abstracts.value: The description of heavy quarks inside the QGP medium, especially at low momenta, remains challenging from first principles, due to large coupling strength and gluon occupation numbers. An alternative way to formulate a description in terms of perturbative degrees of freedom is the interaction of the heavy quarks with the collective excitations of the medium in the form of phonons. This description is derived as an effective field theory (EFT) and therefore allows for a natural occurring power counting of the allowed interactions. This EFT has already been established in our previous work, where we have derived the phonon-heavy quark interactions and calculated their thermal scattering cross section. In this work, we use these results, together with the heavy quark expansion, to calculate the heavy quark drag coefficient. Subsequently, we compare our results with the drag coefficient obtained from AdS/CFT calculations to determine the previously unknown Wilson coefficients for the quark-phonon coupling. Finally, we will use these coefficients to solve the Boltzmann equation for the heavy quark distribution, studying its thermalization in the QGP via soft phonon interactions.

titles.title: Heavy quark thermalization using phonon-heavy quark EFT

abstracts.value: Iterated nonlinear quantum protocols provide a straightforward way of realizing nonlinear dynamics in quantum systems through measurement and postselection. We investigate a family of protocols in which the order of the induced nonlinearity is controlled by the number of qubits involved in a single step. By examining the resulting rational maps and applying a set of numerical diagnostics, we identify extended parameter regions that exhibit ergodic-like dynamics for protocol orders $n=3,4,$ and $5$. We further characterize the associated chaotic behavior through the distribution of Lyapunov exponents. Our results show that ergodic-like dynamics persists beyond the quadratic case, while the geometry of the corresponding parameter regions and the typical degree of chaoticity depend strongly on the order of the nonlinear transformation.

titles.title: Chaos, Fractals, and Ergodicity in Nonlinear Quantum Protocols

abstracts.value: Liouvillian skin effects are usually associated with dissipation whose rates favor unidirectional flow. In this work, we show that directional edge localization can emerge even when population exchange between sites is exactly balanced, with a single tunable phase parameter $α$ deciding their direction and a dual winding structure deciding their nature. Although this number-conserving bath is known for eigenstate selection, we demonstrate here that its phase controls a steady current, which Hamiltonian hopping converts to directional edge localization. Further, we study the spectral winding structure by independently twisting the left (ket) and right (bra) vector indices of the density matrix, revealing two distinct windings whose relationship is dictated by an antiunitary mirror symmetry. Nearest-neighbor jump operators break this symmetry: both windings coincide, giving rise to a common spectral winding $W_0(α)=\pm1$, producing a unipolar skin effect in which the density accumulates at a specific edge. However, next nearest neighbor jump preserve it. The two windings are forced to be opposite, and the ket and bra are pushed to opposite edges, giving a bipolar skin effect of coherences present in eigenmodes, without edge localization of the density in the steady state. Remarkably, in a dimerized chain the phase-controlled density skin effect gives the steady-state zero modes a size-independent weight at the skin edge, accompanied by a kink at the topological transition. In addition, the relaxation time grows linearly with the system size, however at specific phases $α$ where the jump operators are rendered Hermitian, edge-localized eigenmodes with skin character coexist with diffusive relaxation.

titles.title: Phase-Tunable Liouvillian Topology: Dual Winding Structures and Skin Effects

abstracts.value: A measurement of the magnitude of the Cabibbo$-$Kobayashi$-$Maskawa matrix element $V_\mathrm{cb}$ is presented using top quark pair events produced in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV. The data correspond to an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC. The measurement targets the lepton+jets final state, where one W boson decays leptonically and the other hadronically. The value of $\lvert V_\mathrm{cb}\rvert$ is extracted from the branching fraction of the W $\to$ cb decay. To identify this rare signal amid the dominant W $\to$ ud and W $\to$ cs backgrounds, a multivariate discriminant based primarily on the b jet tagging information of the jets assigned to the hadronic W boson decay is used. The measured value is $\lvert V_\mathrm{cb}\rvert$ = [4.59$^{+0.44}_{-0.48}$ (stat) $^{0.64}_{-0.76}$ (syst)] $\times$ 10$^{-2}$. This measurement provides a complementary determination of $\lvert V_\mathrm{cb}\rvert$ at the electroweak scale, independent of the nonperturbative quantum chromodynamics inputs used in measurements based on semileptonic B meson decays.

titles.title: Measurement of the $\lvert V_\mathrm{cb}\rvert$ element of the CKM matrix using $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$ events in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV

abstracts.value: Light-front Quantum Field Theory (LFQFT) stands as an optimal framework for delving into the intricate substructure of hadronic bound states. In this study, we employ a Light-Front Constituent Quark Model (LFCQM) to investigate the pion's internal structure. This model has previously demonstrated significant success in describing the properties of pseudoscalar mesons. A crucial consideration within the light-front formalism is the dependence on the chosen reference frame, stemming from the explicit breaking of covariance. Herein, we meticulously analyze the contribution of zero modes to the pion's electromagnetic current. Subsequently, we explore the impact of these zero modes on observable quantities, including electromagnetic form factors, the pion's electromagnetic radius, and its weak decay constant, $f_π$. Furthermore, we comprehensively investigate the behavior of zero modes and their dependence on both the momentum transfer, $Q^2$, and the model's intrinsic parameters, such as constituent quark masses ($m_{(q,\bar{q})}$) and the regulator mass ($m_R$). Our findings reveal a substantial dependence of light-front zero modes on the specific frame employed for the calculation of the electromagnetic current. Interestingly, we observe that the maximal contribution of the zero mode occurs at a specific four-momentum transfer, denoted as $Q^2 = -q^2 = q_Z^{2(Max.)}$.

titles.title: Behavior of the zero modes in the Light-front for pseudo scalar particles: pion case

abstracts.value: The first experimental study of the dead-cone effect for the charm quark in heavy ion collisions is presented. The analysis is based on a sample of lead-lead (PbPb) collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of 5.02 TeV, recorded by the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC in 2018 and corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 1.7 nb$^{-1}$. The studied observable is the angular distribution of hard, collinear intrajet emissions that are selected with the late-$k_\mathrm{T}$ grooming algorithm. The analysis is performed using inclusive jets and a sample of jets containing prompt D$^0$ mesons. The angular distribution of late-$k_\mathrm{T}$ emissions in PbPb collisions is found to be shifted towards larger angles in D$^0$ jets relative to inclusive jets, indicating a suppression of collinear splittings for D$^0$ jets. This shift, which is expected from the dead-cone effect, is consistent with a similar observation made in proton-proton collisions. The new measurement disfavors hypotheses that predict a filling of the charm-quark dead cone by medium-induced radiation in heavy ion collisions.

titles.title: Probing the charm-quark dead cone effect in heavy ion collisions

abstracts.value: The cuscuton is a scalar field that obeys a constraint rather than an evolution equation, so it modifies gravity without adding a propagating scalar degree of freedom. We study the cosmology of effective cuscuton theory when matter is minimally coupled in the Jordan frame, and therefore conformally coupled to the cuscuton in the Einstein-frame. We derive the background and linear perturbation equations and show that the algebraic cuscuton response mediates a fifth force even though the scalar itself does not propagate. The same conformal factor also changes Einstein-frame particle masses and the friction of matter perturbations, tying the strength and sign of the force to the background evolution rather than to an independent coupling. We study a power-law family of models which contain both tracking solutions and sign-switching solutions; in the latter the effective cuscuton density runs from negative during matter domination to a positive, cosmological-constant-like value today. Using a modified version of CLASS, including the induced particle-mass dependence of recombination, we illustrate the corresponding changes to CMB temperature and linear matter power spectra for benchmark models, without fitting to data. In the strongest benchmarks the fifth force changes the effective gravitational coupling on sub-horizon scales by about one percent, smaller than the accompanying changes to the matter power spectrum and the acoustic scale. For the sign-switching solutions this change is negative over most of cosmic history, so a non-propagating field can weaken rather than strengthen gravitational attraction.

titles.title: Cuscuton Fifth Force: Implications of Non-Dynamical Scalars for Structure Growth

abstracts.value: A thought experiment in the ER=EPR and related literature involves collecting the Hawking radiation of an old black hole, then collapsing it into a second, entangled black hole. In this short note, we examine the resources required by this idealized conversion. More specifically, we are interested in answering the question: how much external energy is needed to form the second black hole? Assuming a semiclassical bound on the information capacity of the newly formed black hole, we derive a conditional lower bound on external energy and a complementary constraint on correlations retained by the exterior degrees of freedom. We also distinguish entropy-level feasibility from the requirements for exact and approximate purification. We illustrate these requirements via a Page curve analysis.

abstracts.value: We show that encoding superconducting qubits as dual-rail or spin-locked transmons lets a metamaterial waveguide couple them all-to-all while suppressing the spurious entanglement that burdens shared-mode architectures, a step toward the non-local connectivity that quantum low-density parity-check codes require. In a bare-transmon architecture, the dispersive coupling between each populated mode and every idle qubit attached to it entangles spectators with the gate, and cancelling it by dynamical decoupling lengthens every gate. The encoding suppresses this coupling at the hardware level, from second to fourth order in the inverse qubit--mode detuning. A two-tone cross-resonance drive then generates a Mølmer-Sørensen interaction between encoded qubits, which we use for an entangling gate and a joint parity measurement, both selective and parallelizable through different modes. Simulating two dual-rail transmons sharing three resonators with a mode lifetime of $30\,μ$s, we find that heralding transmon relaxation as erasure leaves a gate infidelity of $1.4\times10^{-3}$ at $152$~ns, dominated by photon loss. Photon loss and mode crowding together bound the array size. The gate duration must exceed the inverse mode spacing, which shrinks as the array lengthens, while photon loss grows with gate duration. This bound grows linearly with the mode lifetime and with the inter-resonator coupling; at a lifetime of $150\,μ$s, five times the simulated value, and a coupling of $80$~MHz, a $10^{-3}$ error budget admits $13$ qubits on $25$ resonators.

abstracts.value: Repeatedly combining entangling gates on an ensemble of qubits with measurement and postselection on a part of them induces a nonlinear evolution of the unmeasured qubits' state, whose fractal convergence boundaries make the outcome sensitive to the initial state. We study a family of iterated protocols in which $n$ identical qubits are coupled by CNOT gates, $n-1$ of them are postselected, and a parametrized single-qubit unitary acts on the survivor. For orders $n=2$ to $5$, we map the box-counting dimension of the pure-state Julia sets over the complex parameter plane and identify the symmetries that constrain it. Allowing mixed initial states, we find that moderate preparation noise preserves the main parameter-dependent trends of the boundary dimension over much of the studied range, and that the three-dimensional quasi-Julia boundary in the Bloch ball has a dimension that is approximately equal to the dimension of the pure-state Julia set plus one. We further model gate imperfections by an effective depolarizing channel and by fixed coherent interactions. Weak errors leave the estimated dimensions consistent with their ideal values even where the convergence regions visibly deform, and $ZZ$ errors are shown to be exactly conjugate to the ideal protocol at a rotated parameter. Finally, we analyze the postselection and storage cost of an implementation and propose a diagnostic test combining conditional fidelity with acceptance statistics, which we demonstrate on IQM Emerald and Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q.

titles.title: Persistence of Fractal Structures in Iterated Quantum Protocols: Robustness to Preparation and Gate Errors

abstracts.value: In a binary black hole merger, the inspiral portion of the gravitational waveform corresponds to two distinct horizons orbiting each other, and the merger and ringdown signals correspond to the final horizon being formed and settling down to equilibrium. However, we still lack a detailed understanding of the relation between the horizon geometry in these three regimes and the observed waveform. In this thesis, we show that the well-known inspiral chirp waveform has a clear counterpart on black hole horizons, namely the shear of the outgoing null rays at the horizon. The shear behaves very much like a compact binary coalescence waveform with increasing frequency and amplitude, and the parameters of the system estimated from the horizon agree with those estimated from the waveform. We then track the source multipole moments of the dynamical horizons in simulations of several binary black hole mergers and calculate the corresponding Love numbers for axisymmetric modes. Unlike the (field) tidal Love numbers of non-spinning black holes, these do not vanish. We present evidence that, at least for modest mass ratios, their behaviour is universal. We extend this to the non-axisymmetric moments and show that the dynamical horizons encode detailed information about the dynamics of the binary, and that their source multipole moments are strongly correlated with the gravitational field at null infinity. Finally, we study the outer common dynamical horizon formed during the merger and its relationship with the outgoing gravitational waves, and show how the deformed common horizon approaches the final Kerr state by absorbing gravitational radiation with signatures of quasi-normal ringing. Its gravitational field shares a similar multipolar structure as that at future null infinity, and we point out some limitations, inconsistencies, and anomalies that need to be addressed.

titles.title: Strong gravity physics of dynamical horizons in black hole mergers and its imprint in their gravitational radiation

abstracts.value: This study develops and implements a Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) quantum algorithm for solving a one-dimensional linear advection equation with periodic boundary conditions. The governing equation is first discretized using a classical finite difference (FD) scheme to obtain a linear system suitable for quantum solution. We present a newly designed, circuit-level implementation of HHL assembled from Qiskit circuit components and exploit the circulant structure of the periodic discretization matrices through Fourier-based matrix evolution. The HHL algorithm is benchmarked with three explicit schemes and one implicit scheme. The implicit scheme requires a nontrivial linear solve arising from the discretized PDE on progressively finer grids, whereas the explicit schemes provide different input fields for testing state preparation and reconstruction with identity coefficient matrices. HHL solution states are validated against direct classical solves in noiseless simulation. For hardware execution, the periodic matrix structure permits a Fourier implementation that applies reciprocal eigenvalues without phase estimation. Results on the IBM Rensselaer Nighthawk processor are compared at a shared final time. Noiseless reconstructed fields approach the transported profile on resolved grids, while substantial hardware errors remain for both explicit and implicit schemes. Crank-Nicolson remains exceptionally well-conditioned and utilizes similar circuit re sources to the explicit controls, proving that hardware degradation in our tests was not driven by poor matrix conditioning. Ultimately, this study shows new means for HHL algorithms to study quantum CFD problems involving advection equations with implicit time integrations, while demonstrating how state preparation and measurement affect the practical performance of quantum solvers on current devices.

titles.title: Quantum HHL Algorithm for Solving 1D Linear Advection Equation Using Explicit and Implicit Finite Difference Schemes

abstracts.value: Double white dwarfs (DWDs) are important multi-messenger sources and powerful probes of binary interaction physics. Close DWDs formed through isolated binary evolution are expected to have negligible eccentricities. However, recent observations have revealed that some eclipsing DWDs exhibit eccentricities of order $10^{-3}$ or larger. In this work, we investigate the interaction between a circumbinary disk (CBD) and the central DWD, where the CBD is assumed to form from a recent common-envelope (CE) ejection. Our models are the first to include CBD-DWD interaction in DWD population synthesis and to constrain disk parameters such as disk mass and lifetime. Our population models predict a correlation between the eccentricity distribution and the orbital period distribution of DWDs, which can be tested by future observations. Furthermore, we discuss the influence of CBD on the gravitational-wave (GW) signal. The CBD-DWD interaction can shrink the orbit and excite eccentricity, extending the time for which the system is individually resolvable by a future space-borne GW detector. Our results suggest that CBD interaction should be accounted for in population synthesis of Galactic DWD GW sources and the stochastic GW foreground.

titles.title: Double White Dwarfs with Circumbinary Disks: Evolution, Population Properties, and Gravitational Wave Signatures

abstracts.value: We study some geometric aspects behind the Hodges matrix appearing in the context of scattering amplitudes for the $\mathcal N=8$ supergravity. Through a vector bundle construction, we show that the Hodges matrix gives rise to a canonical rational map from the two-step flag variety to symmetric matrices, called the $\textit{Hodges map}$. This construction allows to define the amplitude geometrically: its vanishing locus is a divisor - the $\textit{MHV gravity divisor}$. Inspired by the Hodges map, we introduce the notion of Hadamard ratio of two varieties. In the case relevant to gravity, this is the ratio of two Grassmannians, which we call the $\textit{pentad variety}$, connecting it to the pentad constraint from algebraic statistics. Moreover, we show that the pentad variety is closely related to the combinatorial algebraic geometry of Martin's affine slope variety, and the phirotopes of Below, Krummeck, and Richter-Gebert.

titles.title: From MHV Gravity Amplitudes and Hodges map to Pentad Varieties

abstracts.value: We present Aurora, a black hole seeding module for the Mimic semi-analytic framework, in which the seed mass of each newly resolved halo is set by its environment. Motivated by evidence that early quiescent galaxies and overmassive black holes assemble in dense environments, Aurora replaces the fixed seed masses of conventional prescriptions with a continuous spectrum, coupling the seed mass to two environmental parameters, the local overdensity and the radial skewness of the surrounding haloes, and to the halo mass at seeding. Requiring only halo masses and positions, it applies to dark-matter-only simulations. Calibrated against Sage on the Millennium merger trees, this prescription leaves a lasting signal. Massive black holes are assembled from the seeds of many progenitors, seeds supplying 29 per cent of all black hole mass formed by $z=0$. A seed-dominated growth pathway, distinct from the accretion-dominated majority, emerges among galaxies assembled rapidly in dense, asymmetric environments. Environment-dependent seeding raises the quiescent fraction of seeded galaxies in massive haloes at $z \simeq 3.1$ by up to 70 per cent, with the excess concentrated in overdense environments, and a deficit in voids. Scrambling the seeding environments while preserving the mass spectrum erases this gradient. The two environmental couplings imprint separable signatures, broadening the scatter of the galaxy-black hole mass relation while preserving the stellar-halo mass relation and other Sage summary statistics. We discuss applying Aurora at gigaparsec scales and higher resolution, to understand the origins of massive black hole systems in contemporary deep surveys.

titles.title: Introducing Aurora: A New Black Hole Seeding Model With Explicit Environmental Coupling

abstracts.value: We propose a hierarchical scale-bridging construction for building first principles electronic structure models of extended molecular aggregates with disorder, and its practical realization in exciton systems. The general construction, referred here as to the encapsulation, is based on a recursive operator-valued hierarchy cast in a dual graph-theoretic (discrete) and configuration-space (continuous) structure, in which variables associated with a coarser level parameterize operators governing the degrees of freedom at the next finer level in a graph-covariant, geometry-preserving fashion. In an exemplary application of this scheme, aggregate-level ground- and excited-state operators are constructed through a many-body expansion (MBE), with matrix elements evaluated in a basis comprising the aggregate ground state and local Frenkel excitations. The required monomer and dimer building blocks are obtained from DFT and TDDFT calculations, yielding aggregate-level 1-particle transition density matrices as well as Hamiltonian, dipole moment and other operators that can be evaluated at the level of the building blocks. Starting from structural models obtained from experiment or molecular dynamics, this approach generates aggregate-level operators in a bottom-up fashion without fitting parameters to spectroscopic data or performing calculations on larger system cutouts. A numerical demonstration is given for an excitonic manifold in crystalline quaterthiophene. In particular, through its intrinsic configuration-dependence encoded in the encapsulations, it will provide a bridge between static electronic structure calculations for realistic, structurally disordered aggregates and quantum or quantum-classical simulations of exciton-vibrational dynamics.

titles.title: Graph-Covariant Bottom-Up Scale-Bridging Reconstruction of Ground and Excited States of Extended Systems

abstracts.value: The theoretical description of the ultrafast optical response of nitrogen-vacancy centers has traditionally been developed using the nonlinear response function formalism based on a displaced harmonic oscillator model. However, restrictive defect geometries that lead to rich phonon mode distributions can limit the validity of this model. Here, we extend this framework by incorporating state-dependent oscillator modes characterized by different frequencies. We demonstrate that, as a consequence, the nonlinear response function is modified by a straightforward correction term that can be evaluated using operator algebraic techniques. These modifications directly impact two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy, which serves as a vital characterization tool for color centers by resolving ultrafast correlated electron-vibrational dynamics.

titles.title: Theoretical estimation of nonlinear response function and ultrafast optical spectroscopy of nitrogen vacancy centers

abstracts.value: Dynamical decoupling suppresses decoherence by averaging selected interactions between a quantum system and its environment. Here, we extend this notion through a general Floquet formalism that maps periodic control onto relaxation and dephasing channels. Environmental fluctuations are decomposed into Floquet components that sample the noise spectrum at distinct frequencies, with coupling strengths determined by control-induced Floquet coefficients. We experimentally investigate this approach using a single nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under multi-pulse control. By tuning the drive and detuning, we reshape the coupling to environmental fluctuations and create isolated operating points where the dominant decoherence channel vanishes, strongly suppressing Floquet dephasing. The resulting coherence enhancement follows the predicted Floquet coupling coefficients and can be shifted by modifying the control sequence. These results establish Floquet driving as a general framework for engineering transverse and longitudinal relaxation through the design of quantum control protocols.

titles.title: Floquet engineering of quantum relaxation

abstracts.value: We present a native transverse-momentum realization of the Collins/CSS2 leading-power transverse-momentum-dependent (TMD) factorization framework. The construction connects fixed-order distributional matching, origin contacts, unexpanded two-scale evolution, and a differentiable interface for hadronic structure. An endpoint-independent canonical scale with a specified infrared completion generates a Collins--Soper kernel on a common invariant domain. Complete canonical legs are bounded and admit constructive momentum-space evaluation through resolvent convolutions or elliptic solves. We give contact and finite-bin error bounds, parent-to-momentum-boundary translations, ordered flavor recurrences, and an all-order argument for the four exponent towers of $N^3\mathrm{LL}$ evolution. Localized joint-$(x,k_T)$ inputs, nonperturbative rapidity broadening, regulated moments and the full-spectrum subtraction are formulated as distinct parts of the prescription. The physical realization uses sourced four-loop beta/cusp and three-loop noncusp/Collins--Soper ingredients with strict-NLO hard/OPE boundaries. Non-Gaussian continuum tests and three-scale physical-PDF comparisons validate ordinary legs, contacts, individual insertions and analytic input derivatives. Including a declared bound on the continuation above a finite PDF table, physical bin discrepancies remain below $4.27\times10^{-5}$ of the peak reference bin. A qualified proton--proton Drell--Yan and neural-closure demonstration connects the method to inverse use. Higher-order boundary assembly and matched observables are specified without claiming an implemented $N^3\mathrm{LL}'$ spectrum or a completed global extraction.

titles.title: Native transverse-momentum evolution and matching for TMD factorization and extraction

Abstract

Cosmological observations show that dark matter (DM), which has virtually no electro-
magnetic interactions but which is about five times more abundant than familiar “baryonic”
matter, must exist. A well-motivated hypothesis postulates the existence of WIMPs (Weakly
Interacting Massive Particles) as DM. These particles are thought to interact with (some)
known particles with a strength roughly corresponding to the known weak interactions.
This renders experimental searches for these particles viable, in particular through elastic
scattering on nuclei in a terrestrial detector. For many years, the relevant interaction of
WIMPs with protons and neutrons was described by two parameters in each case. These
parameters give rise to interactions where the WIMP coupling to the nucleus is independent
of nuclear spin and where the WIMP coupling is dependent on nuclear spin. However, it
has recently been pointed out, in view of a non-relativistic effective field theory (NREFT)
construction, that more than 20 additional parameters could play a role here, which would
make interpreting the experimental results significantly more challenging. These additional
NREFT parameters describe interactions between WIMP and nuclei which were previously
not known. This thesis addresses the question whether the additionally introduced NREFT
parameters can play a significant role in describing WIMP-nucleus scattering and which
among the additional parameters may be retained along with the traditional approach of using
two parameters. In particular, focus herein is directed towards examining such questions for
those NREFT parameters which violate discrete symmetries such as Parity (P) and Time
Reversal (T). Simplified models, which respect only part of the SM gauge symmetries, have
been suggested for generating such P- and T-violating parameters. We have analyzed the
interplay of constraints from neutron electric dipole moment (nEDM) searches and direct DM
searches for such simplified models. We find that for the majority of scenarios considered,
the subleading NREFT parameters can be safely ignored and WIMP-nucleus scattering is
sufficiently well described by the older approach of retaining two parameters. This is not
surprising since the two parameters are actually zeroth order terms of the NREFT construction
and the newly introduced parameters are higher order correction terms. We further identify
scenarios where one of the subleading NREFT parameters can be more relevant than the two
zeroth order NREFT parameters. Our results provide an improved understanding of the whole
set of NREFT parameters and clarify their relevance for analysing experimental searches.

CHAPTER 1

The Standard Model of Particle Physics

The Standard Model (SM) is a local, relativistic and renormalizable quantum field theory which
respects three different gauge symmetries [3–8]. The three gauge symmetries are responsible
for describing three known fundamental interactions — strong, weak and electromagnetic
interactions.

The SM’s raison d’etre is a description of all the elementary particles and their interactions.
This description in the SM is in the language of quantum fields, whose excitations constitute
particles and whose interactions, among themselves and between each other, lead to inter-
actions of the particles. The SM fields have well defined transformations under the gauge
symmetries, and consequently, only those interactions of the SM fields are allowed which
respect gauge symmetries. In addition, the SM fields respect a global spacetime symmetry,
described by the (restricted) Poincare group.

The local, or gauge, symmetries of the SM can be written as the following direct product
of three distinct gauge groups,

1.2 Successes of the SM
The predictive power of the SM is truly remarkable. With its 23 parameters, the SM as a
theory makes predictions which are in excellent agreement with a multitude of experimental
data [15]. Particularly in the electroweak sector, the predictions of the SM have been tested
successfully to a very high precision [16].

The discovery of the Higgs boson by the ATLAS [17] and the CMS [18] experiments in
2012 verified the last missing piece from the SM’s particle spectrum. Not only the Higgs,
but the confirmed predictions of the 𝑊± bosons and the 𝑍 boson [19], the top quark [20,
21] and the tau neutrino [22] have added to the credibility of the SM as a robust theoretical
framework for describing the fundamental building blocks of nature.

In particular, the SM prediction for the anomalous magnetic dipole moment of the
electron [23] agrees with experimental data at a precision of one part in a trillion [24]. The
fine structure constant, 𝛼−1

= ℏ𝑐/𝑒2 has also been tested to one part in a billion [25–28].
To the astonishment of many physicists, there is no clear discrepancy persisting between

SM predictions and the high energy data collected by ATLAS and CMS experiments at
the LHC after many years in operation. As a result, the SM has been verified for energies√
𝑠 = 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity reaching more than 150 fb−1 [15].
The SM also successfully describes the known early history of the universe. The Standard

1.3 Shortcomings of the SM
Among particle physicists, it is generally well acknowledged that the SM, despite its predictive
successes, constitutes an incomplete description of nature. In the following, we list some of
the salient issues plaguing the SM.

• Gravity: The SM provides an unifying picture of three of the four known fundamental
forces, viz. the strong and the weak forces along with electromagnetism. However, a
satisfying description of the gravitational force at the quantum level is missing in the
SM. In other words, a UV completion of gravity which in the low-energy limit reduces
to the SM remains elusive. Although string theory is a compelling candidate for such a
description, its connection to the SM has not yet been identified.

• Dark Matter: Slightly more than a quarter of the mass-energy content of the universe
is attributed to Dark Matter (DM) in the standard model of cosmology (ΛCDM).
Gravitational evidence for DM has been accumulating since the 1930s [35]. The SM
alone cannot account for particle DM. We review this shortcoming of the SM in further
detail in chapter 2.

• Dark Energy: In ΛCDM cosmology, a cosmological constant Λ which dominates the
total energy density of the universe is required to explain observations that the universe
is presently accelerating. Although the cosmological constant is a mathematically
and physically simple theoretical explanation, its unnaturally small magnitude is a
major conundrum. The energy density of Λ, which can be interpreted as a measure
of the energy density of the vacuum, is inferred from cosmological observations to be
10−47 GeV4. The vacuum energy density computed using the particle physics input,
i.e. the zero point energy of quantum fields of the SM yields a vacuum energy density
around 10−8 GeV4. This discrepancy spanning 54 orders of magnitude is known as the
“cosmological constant problem" [36]. A convincing solution for this problem is not
known [37].

• Baryogenesis: The existence of anti-particles is a fundamental prediction of relativistic
QFTs, which has been confirmed by many SM anti-particle discoveries. This notwith-
standing, the observable universe seems to be overwhelmingly dominated by matter
instead of antimatter. The cosmic matter-antimatter asymmetry is parameterized by the
net density of baryons scaled by the density of photons, which is inferred to be rather
small, 𝜂 ∼ 10−10. In order to produce this net baryon asymmetry, Sakharov reasoned
three conditions to be essential [38]: baryon number violation, 𝐶 and 𝐶𝑃 violation, and
a departure from thermal equilibrium. The third condition is not difficult to realize in
an expanding universe. Baryon number is not conserved by the non-perturbative sector
of the SM and CP is clearly violated in the SM. Although an expanding universe and
the SM technically fulfill Sakharov’s conditions, the amount of CP violation present in
the SM is far from sufficient to account for baryogenesis.

• Flavour problems: A large fraction of the parameters of the SM pertain to flavor. In
particular, the lepton and quark masses must be taken as input parameters without an
understanding as to why they span many orders of magnitude [39]. Roughly speaking,
matter is only made of electrons, up quarks and down quarks. Therefore, if the SM
were to be an economical and fitting description, additional families of fermions would
actually be superfluous. The question then arises as to why additional families of
fermions are present in the SM, and further as to why this number is restricted to three.
For further details, see Refs. [40–43].

• Neutrino masses: Experiments [44] have shown that neutrinos oscillate. These
oscillations are explained by nonzero neutrino masses and mixing among neutrino flavor
eigenstates [12, 45, 46]. Recall that the SM contains only left-handed neutrino fields
and thus SM by itself does not account for massive neutrinos. In the most economical
scenarios, writing down a Dirac mass term for the neutrino necessitates the introduction
of right handed neutrino fields while a Majorana mass term for the neutrinos violates
lepton number, a conserved quantity in the SM.

• Inflation: The observed flatness of the universe requires extremely fine tuned initial
conditions in big bang cosmology. This fine tuning is ameliorated by positing that
the universe underwent a phase of exponentially rapid expansion, known as cosmic
inflation [47, 48]. The expansion is assumed to be driven by the energy density of a
scalar field (usually) called the inflaton. This rapid expansion is then followed by a
phase of reheating [49, 50], wherein the potential energy of the inflaton is converted
to thermalised SM particles therewith recovering a hot, thermal, radiation-dominated
universe. It appears unlikely that the SM fields alone can account for inflation.

• Hierarchy Problem: In the SM, quantum corrections to fermion and gauge boson
masses are proportional to the corresponding particle masses themselves. These mass
parameters are said to be technically natural [51] since they are protected by a symmetry
(a chiral symmetry for the fermions and a gauge symmetry for the gauge bosons, both

Before culminating this section, it is interesting to point out that the SM lacks consistency

scale is considerably smaller than the energy scale associated with the Landau pole of QED,
it is often conjectured that a quantum theory of gravity would rectify this.

Another issue worth mentioning is the strong CP problem [59–61] originating in the QCD
sector of the SM. The SM contains a theta term, 𝜃 𝐺 ·𝐺̃,which breaks both 𝑃−, 𝐶𝑃−symmetries

even though the rest of the QCD Lagrangian does not break 𝑃 or𝐶𝑃 [62]. nEDM searches [63,

extremely fine-tuned. In other words, it is not clear as to why the SM lacks flavour-diagonal

problem involves dynamically setting the 𝜃 term to zero with help of a pseudoscalar field,
referred to as the axion [65–68]. Searches for the axion have not yielded any positive results
so far.

To summarize, the aforementioned list of shortcomings of the SM are, by no means,
exhaustive. For a comprehensive list of questions that can be posed which the SM may not be
able to convincingly answer, the reader is referred to Ref. [69].

separated by a distance ®𝑟, the electric dipole moment (EDM) ®𝑑 is given by the product of

In quantum mechanics, for a particle at rest, the expectation value of the dipole moment
operator ⟨𝑑⟩ is proportional to the particle’s spin ®𝑠. In other words, the EDM of the particle
must either be parallel or anti-parallel to its intrinsic angular momentum (spin) ®𝑠.

Under parity 𝑃, the dipole moment ®𝑑 changes sign while spin ®𝑠 does not. This means
that either the dipole moment ®𝑑 vanishes or 𝑃 is broken, i.e. 𝑃 is not a valid symmetry of
the particle. A similar argument can be applied for time reversal 𝑇 . Under time reversal 𝑇 ,
the dipole moment ®𝑑 does not change sign while spin ®𝑠 does. As before, either the dipole
moment ®𝑑 vanishes or 𝑇 is not a valid symmetry of the particle. Therefore, a finite EDM
of an elementary particle would indicate that P and T discrete symmetries are violated [70].
The CPT theorem states that a quantum field theory which is local, unitary and Lorentz
invariant must be invariant under the combined CPT symmetry [71, 72]. This implies that the
observation of a nonzero value of a permanent EDM would signal the existence of interactions
violating CP symmetry.

CP violation is already present in the SM due to: the strong CP phase 𝜃, the CP violating
phase in the CKM quark mixing matrix, and a similar phase as the CKM phase in the PMNS
lepton mixing matrix. The CKM and PMNS phases arise from an interplay of the three
fermion families. Consequently their contribution to flavor diagonal CP violation probes,
such as EDMs, is rather small — many order of magnitude below sensitivities of ongoing
and future planned EDM experiments. Due to the smallness of CKM and PMNS CPV
contributions, EDMs offer an alternate way, compared to collider searches, of searching for
CP violating interactions arising in numerous BSM extensions. In fact, the current sensitivity
level already probes mass scales which are considerably higher than those accessible via

Experiments searching for an EDM must be carried out carefully to not allow spurious
electric field effects from interfering in measurements. A systematic effect which has plagued
experiments in the past relates to small leakage currents generating magnetic fields which are
then correlated with the electric field. This gives rise to an additional term in the Hamiltonian
of eq. (1.20) which is proportional to the electric field ®𝐸 and thus cannot be distinguished
from the EDM signal. See [74] for more details.

An appreciation for the complexity of the “table-top" EDM experiments can be gained
from the order of magnitude of the precession frequency involved in the measurement. In
the Earth’s magnetic fieldii, a neutron has a precession frequency of around 9000 s−1 due to
its magnetic moment 𝜇. If an EDM of 10−26 e · cm is assumed, then for a typical electric
field involved in EDM experiments 𝐸 ∼ 107 V/m, the precession frequency is roughly
10−6 − 10−7 s−1, which is at least 10 orders of magnitude smaller!

The accuracy with which the shift in precession frequency can be measured is inversely
proportional to the time that the system interacts with the applied electric field [74, 75].
Therefore, in order to increase sensitivity, experiments aim to increase the duration of the
measurement. Further, the shift in the precession frequency scales linearly with the electric
field. Thus, experimental collaborations also strive to use stronger electric fields for improving
sensitivity.

As the name suggests, galaxy clusters are gravitationally bound structures comprising
a number of galaxiesiii of the order O(103 − 104) [106]. Galaxies in a galaxy cluster are
in equilibrium and their dynamics are fairly non-relativistic. Therefore, by virtue of the
virial theorem one can measure the peculiar velocities of the galaxies bound in a cluster
(thus providing a measure of the cluster’s kinetic energy) and therewith determine the total
mass bound in the cluster, provided the size of the cluster is known [107, 108]. This is in
accordance with what was done for the Coma cluster by Fritz Zwicky in 1933 [35]. He
further assumed the Coma cluster contained a similar number of stars as a typical nebula,
which was well known at the time, and derived a mass-to-light ratio for the Coma cluster to
be around 500 𝑀⊙/𝐿⊙, in units of the solar mass divided by the solar luminosity. To account
for the astonishingly high mass-to-light ratio, he postulated the presence of non-luminous,
i.e., dark matter within the Coma cluster. In other words, some missing mass was necessary
for the Coma cluster to be in equilibrium. A similar analysis for the Virgo cluster was carried
out by Smith slightly later in 1936 [109].

Although we have described the gravitational evidence for non-luminous matter in virialized

The much-discussed bullet cluster (1E 0657-558)iv concerns a pair of galaxy clusters - a
main cluster and a smaller sub-cluster which passed through each other around ∼ 100 Myr
ago [120]. Optical observations of the bullet cluster [121] together with reconstruction of the
gravitational potential using weak lensing [122] show that the mass of the bullet cluster is
concentrated around the main cluster and the smaller sub-cluster. However, X-ray observations
of emissions of the hot gas, which forms most of the clusters’ baryonic mass, show that
the hot gas has undergone deceleration and slowed down compared to the galaxies [116].
This discrepancy is illustrated in Figure 2.2 by way of the spatial separation between the
equipotential contours inferred by weak lensing observations and the shock waves of the hot
gas inferred from X-ray emission spectra of the bullet cluster. Like earlier, this missing mass
problem can be resolved by hypothesizing the presence of non-luminous matter present in the
galaxies. Therefore, the bullet cluster provides a unique astronomical context in which the
observed baryonic components and the hypothesized non-luminous components of galaxies
are spatially segregated.

Measurements of temperature anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background (Δ𝑇/𝑇)𝑙>1 ≃
10−5 show that density perturbations at the time of recombinationv were rather small, peaking
at roughly 1 part in 10,000, 𝛿𝜌/𝜌 < 10−4 [15, 107, 123–126]. General relativity predicts that
the amplitude of such density perturbations must necessarily grow with the scale factor 𝑎,
𝛿𝜌/𝜌 < 10−4, since the onset of matter domination in the universe. Since the scale factor
has only grown by a factor of ∼ 103 since recombination, the density perturbations are far
too small to form the observed structures of the universe, i.e. the density fluctuations must
be significantly greater than one, 𝛿𝜌/𝜌 ≫ 1 [127]. Ergo, in a baryon-only universe there
is not enough time for structures to grow sufficiently, i.e., non-linearly. Therefore, some
mechanism which allows matter domination to begin earlier in the universe, and therewith
seeds the formation of structures in the universe, is required. The presence of non-luminous
non-baryonic matter, with significant larger density perturbations at the time of recombination
and having decoupled from the baryon-photon plasma at least before recombination, thus
allows for large scale structures to be timely formed [107, 112, 127].

In order to form structures in the universe, this non-luminous non-baryonic matter must
have a small thermal velocity compared to the speed of light at the time of matter-radiation

act of clustering is expected to heat up the surrounding non-luminous non-baryonic matter
ensemble, this heating is not expected to be significant for altering its thermal velocity. In
cosmological parlance, this feature of the non-luminous non-baryonic matter is referred to as
being “cold” [128, 129]. It is worth pointing out that this is true at cosmological scales, but
not expected to be true everywhere. For instance, in the vicinity of a compact object such as

We now discuss how DM can obtain a correct value of abundance matching observations -
one of the required properties discussed in the previous chapter. Roughly speaking, there are
around four categories in which mechanisms for producing DM in the early universe can be
classified: thermal, non-thermal, asymmetric, and gravitation-based [238–240].

The first category, which happens to be the simplest and oldest of the four, of thermal
mechanisms has been the subject of much attention in the literature [241, 242]. These
mechanisms rely on the assumption that the particle species in consideration is in thermal
equilibrium with the surrounding plasma in the universe and has zero chemical potential
(that is, the particle species participates in creation and annihilation processes at equal rates).
Among such mechanisms, thermal freeze-out, or thermal decoupling has enjoyed extensive
scrutiny, which is mainly due to the fact that the mechanism of thermal freeze-out, or thermal
decoupling, has been involved in successful predictions of recombination (in the context
of CMB) and BBN, and further provides a convincing picture of cosmological neutrino
decoupling [243].

The idea of thermal decoupling is simple. As the universe expands, it cools down and the
number density of a given particle species decreases. Eventually the rate Γ for the species’
number changing processes, which maintained thermal equilibrium, becomes smaller than
the expansion rate of the universe, given by 𝐻. At this point in time (or temperature), the

Hot relics are highly disfavored to constitute DM by themselves owing to issues in large
scale structure formation [127]. Adiabatic density fluctuations, which eventually grow to form
large scale structure, are erased, or "washed-out", due to free streaming of the hot relics. This
results in a suppression of the matter power spectrum at small scales, which is in conflict with
the inferred matter power spectrum from various cosmological observations [130, 249–253].
Further, hot relics lead to a "top-down" structure formation where larger structures such
as galactic superclusters or clusters are formed prior to galaxies [254, 255]. Hot relics are
then controverted by the observations of galaxies at redshift 𝑧 ∼ 3 and of massive galaxy
clusters at redshift 𝑧 ∼ 2, indicating galaxies must have formed earlier than galaxy clusters.
Additionally N-body numerical simulations of hot relics as DM indicate that hot relics face
trouble in forming galaxies [256]. A canonical example of a hot relic is the SM neutrino, and
is therefore no longer a viable DM candidate particle being ruled out as a standalone DM
particle by negative search results [257].

3.2 Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs)

Co-annihilations concern scenarios where WIMPs are accompanied by another non-SM
stable massive particle species 𝑌 , which is nearly mass degenerate with the WIMP, in the
course of decoupling from the thermal plasma. In such scenarios, in addition to WIMP
self-annihilations (WIMP + WIMP→ Plasma) and the self-annihilations of species 𝑌 (Y +
Y→ Plasma), the co-annihilations of the WIMP and the species 𝑌 into the thermal plasma
(WIMP + Y→ Plasma) can greatly affect the eventual WIMP relic abundance [265–269].

Although thermal WIMPs in standard cosmology have been the focus of the discussion
in this chapter, it is worth mentioning that WIMPs also can be produced non-thermally in
the universe, where WIMPs being in chemical and kinetic equilibrium with the thermal
plasma is no longer assumed [237, 270, 271]. In such cases, WIMPs can be produced by
some out-of-equilibrium process. Scenarios where the DM particle species never thermalize
with the SM plasma owing to its highly suppressed interactions with the SM plasma and
eventually accumulate in the universe by collisions or decays of the thermal bath are known
as freeze-in [272–274] and can be viewed as an opposite paradigm of producing DM in
the universe relative to freeze-out. Further, various modifications to standard cosmology
incorporating thermal WIMPs or other DM candidates abound in the literature.

The prevalence of WIMPs in a variety of BSM theories comprises a crucial motivation for
WIMPs. This motivation is strengthened by the fact these BSM theories are not contrived
to generate WIMPs. Au contraire, these BSM theories are formulated to address field-
theoretic/particle physics deficiencies of the SM, such as the hierarchy problem. Therefore,
WIMPs are supported by motivations of the BSM theory in which they naturally appear
independently of the DM hypothesis. Although not all extensions of the SM are well motivated
(some of which may even be formulated to address a transient experimental anomaly), these
are still favorable over SM extensions which can at best be described as constructed ad hoc to
account for DM.

The WIMP paradigm gained further prominence from the realization that such particles
could be probed in different categories of experiments [275, 276]. The prospect of detectability
in combination with independent theoretical particle physics motivations has been the
justification of the extensive scrutiny that WIMPs have so far received. Three different
categories of experiments which can detect WIMPs are termed as direct searches, indirect
searches and collider searches.

Direct searches utilize the idea that there is an appreciable amount of WIMP flux on earth
and hence WIMPs can scatter off target nuclei in detectors giving rise to signals [276]. The
principle behind direct searches was actually first suggested to detect neutrinos scattering
elastically off nuclei [277], the same process which forms a persistent SM background for
WIMP signals at small WIMP-nucleus cross-sections. For instance, the oldest WIMP - a
fourth-generation neutrino with massv 𝑚𝜈 > 𝑚𝑍/2 was cast aside as a DM candidate owing
to null results from the first direct detection experiments [278, 279]. Current experiments
constrain the mass of this fourth-generation neutrino to be at least O(TeV), implying that it

Indirect searches rely on the detection of annihilation products of WIMPs self-annihilation
in the Milky Way [275, 280–283], the same process which occurs in the early universe and
accounts for the observed relic abundance. The one great advantage that indirect searches
have is that the annihilation products are SM particles which can be detected relatively easily.
Typical annihilation products relevant for indirect detection include charged particles such as
electron and positrons, protons and antiprotons, deuterium and anti-deuterium; photons in
the form of gamma rays, X-rays and synchroton radiation; and neutrinos. However, indirect
detection strategies are limited by astrophysical backgrounds (and foregrounds) which are
hard to model sufficiently accurately and thus contribute to significant systematic errors. A

4.1 Obtaining the matrix element of DM-nucleus scattering

4.1 Obtaining the matrix element of DM-nucleus
scattering

Postulating the kind of interactions that DM has with SM particles is essential towards
obtaining the matrix element of DM-nucleus scattering. In the scope of this thesis, the
discussion is restricted to a DM particle interacting with SM quarks. There are different
degrees of specificity that one can choose in describing DM-quark interactions. The most
specific of such descriptions involves writing down a fully SM-gauge invariant theory, or
partially SM-gauge invariant theory, comprising at least one DM candidate. Examples of
such theories which are compelling, for reasons not just limited to the presence of viable DM
candidates, are supersymmetric extensions of the SM. Lagrangians of such theories usually
contain different kinds of DM-quark interactions.

Calculating the DM-nucleus cross section thus involves three steps. A first step involves
calculating effective interactions of DM between quarks and gluons, wherein the effective
interactions depends on parameters present in the underlying theory. A second step involves
promoting the quark-level effective interactions into interactions with nucleons. This is done
by evaluating the matrix elements of quark and/or gluon operators between initial and final
nucleon states. Here the distribution of quarks and gluons bound in the nucleon become
important. A third step involves evaluating the nucleonic matrix elements between nuclear
states. In this step, the distribution of nucleons in the nucleus plays a crucial role.

Another specific description of DM-quark interactions involves writing down relativistic
effective DM-quark or effective DM-nucleon interactions while being agnostic about the
underlying fundamental theory. The DM-nucleus scattering matrix element can then
be obtained as described in the step-wise procedure. Although this approach is model-
independent, it may conceal relevance of different effective operators relative to each other
which may be apparent in a full fledged theory or even in a simplified model.

We now follow the less specific approach and describe a few relativistic effective DM-quark
operators. These operators have facilitated a classification of DM-nuclei interactions into
broadly two categories — spin independent (SI) and spin dependent (SD) interactions. In
the former category, DM couples to the mass of the nucleus (and being independent of the
nuclear spin) and in the latter category, DM couples to the spin of the nucleus.

4.2 Experimental searches
Direct detection experiments are optimized to observe signals arising from DM scattering
off target nuclei in a detector. These signals are small, having energies ≲ O(keV), and rare,

58



4.2 Experimental searches

with the numbers of events ∼ 1 event/kg yr. The energy deposited in the target nuclei gives
rise to ionization, scintillation or lattice vibrations (as phonons) in the detector, which are
then converted to measurable signals. Recent experiments exploit a combination of two of
the three detection channels improving upon the older experiments which were restricted
to using a single channel. The use of two detection channels allows experiments to to
distinguish between electron recoils (ERs) and nuclear recoils (NRs), thereby achieving a
greater sensitivity. This is because for typical models with GeV-scale DM, a NR signal are
are far more likely to be induced than an ER signal.

Chapter 4 Direct detection of Dark Matter

Due to the rare and feeble nature of DM signals, reducing background to the degree where
DM signals can be cleanly observed is a daunting task. Since the first set of experiments in the
80s, much effort has been expended towards achieving ultra-low background conditions. The
first step in background reduction involves reducing cosmic and environmental radiation by
operating detectors in suitable locations, such as in deep underground laboratories [332]. In
addition to being low-radioactive environments, detectors in these locations typically receive
a significantly smaller cosmic ray flux because of being at large depths below the Earth’s
surface. Neutrons, in particular, are a problematic source of background since they can
induce NRs similar to DM. Cosmic ray muons, for instance, produce showers of GeV-scale
neutrons from spallation reactions with the surroundings. To reduce the neutron-induced NR
background and other cosmic rays related background, the detector volume is surrounded
by shielding structures, such as large lead or water tanks, which are used to tag and remove
events associated with muons and neutrons.

The next step of background reduction involves reducing radioactive impurities which
are present in the detector components or could be attached to their surfaces [333]. This is
taken care of by selecting radio-pure materials for building the detector components and by
removing surface contaminants. Contamination from radioactive isotopes, such as Radon
and Krypton isotopes can be particularly challenging and experiments have developed special
techniques for their removal [334].

An eventual background for all direct detection experiments comes from neutrinos in the
form of the solar neutrinos, the atmospheric neutrinos and the diffuse supernovae background
(DSNB). Neutrinos can scatter on nuclei inducing nuclear recoils, closely resembling DM
induced nuclear recoils. Unlike other backgrounds, neutrinos cannot be shielded or rejected
since there is no means of tagging them in direct search experiments. The solar neutrinos form
the dominant background for DM-nucleus scattering for low DM masses 𝑚𝜒 ≤ 10 GeV while
the atmospheric and diffuse supernova background neutrinos are more relevant for larger
DM masses. A lower limit on the discoverable DM-nucleon cross section, that is, a value
of the DM-nucleon cross section where the neutrino nucleus scattering is still subdominant
to DM-nucleus scattering, is called the neutrino floor [277, 335–338]. This lower limit is
especially sensitive to uncertainties in the neutrino flux. Although the use of high statistics
has been invoked for circumventing the overwhelming neutrino background, directional
detection in combination with other approaches may at best probe DM-nucleon cross section
only up to a few times smaller than the neutrino floor [339]. It is therefore justified to express
that, at least at the time of writing, the neutrino background forms an irreducible background
for continually probing smaller DM-nucleon cross sections.

At the time of writing, a positive DM signaliii has not been observed by various direct
search experiments. Therefore, in light of null results, direct search experiments place upper
limits on the DM-nucleon cross sections 𝜎𝜒𝑁 as a function of DM mass 𝑚𝜒. The upper
limits are usually displayed as an exclusion plot in the 𝜎𝜒𝑁 − 𝑚𝜒 plane. Figures 4.2 and 4.3
display the current upper limits on the DM-nucleon SI and SD cross sections respectively

Non-relativistic effective field theory

In the previous chapter, we computed the DM-nucleus cross section assuming certain four-
field DM-quark effective operators. These DM-quark effective operators ultimately lead
to the standard SI and SD interactions between DM and nucleons. Both these interactions
are independent of momentum transfer ®𝑞 and relative DM-nucleon velocity ®𝑣 in the non-
relativistic limit, and thus have finite contributions to the DM-nucleus cross section in the
limit of vanishing DM velocity, ®𝑣 → 0.

Other “contact" effective operators had not been considered because their contributions
to the DM-nucleus cross section vanish as ®𝑣 → 0 (which implies ®𝑞 → 0 as well)! In
particular, effective operators involving scalar- and pseudoscalar-DM and quark currents lead
to DM-nucleus cross sections being suppressed by powers of momentum transfer ®𝑞. For
example, the scalar-pseudoscalar (S-PS) effective operator 𝜒̄𝜒 𝑞𝑖𝛾5

the NR limit.

Another reason for the lack of attention that such operators have received, at least in regard
to well-motivated extensions of the SM, stems from the expectation that even at non-zero ®𝑞,
the ®𝑞− or ®𝑣−dependent interactions would still be subdominant to the ®𝑞− or ®𝑣−independent
interactions. Especially, scenarios where the ®𝑞− or ®𝑣−independent interactions could be
suppressed, or made to vanish entirely, thereby leaving the ®𝑞− or ®𝑣−independent interactions
as the dominant contributions to the cross section, were prima facie seen as contrived and
unlikely [260].

DM-nucleus scattering. It has been argued, in Refs. [346, 348], that previously ignored
interactions, viz. ®𝑞− and/or ®𝑣− dependent interactions, naturally emerge when the relevant

CHAPTER 6

Summary and Conclusions

It is clear from astrophysical and cosmological observations that DM is abundant in the
Universe, as detailed in chapter 2. Strikingly, the SM — the standard framework of particle
physics which explains ‘normal’ matter remarkably well, can not account for DM as a particle
without modifications, as indicated in chapter 1. Such modifications usually extendi the
particle content of the SM so as to comprise a DM candidate. A well studied category of
DM candidates is WIMPs, which were discussed in chapter 3. Since the 1980s, WIMPs have
been extensively sought in direct searches. Direct search experiments rely on the expectation
that WIMPs bound in the Milky Way halo scatter with nuclei causing them to recoil, thereby
generating detectable signals; this was the subject of discussion in chapter 4.

A long-standing consideration in describing WIMP-nucleus scattering is to consider WIMP-
quark interactions only of the form which lead to SI and SD WIMP-nucleus interactions,
the former independent of nuclear spin and the latter depending on it. The chief reasons
behind considering only SI and SD interactions are two-fold. First, most well-motivated
SM extensions contain, without contrivance, the requisite WIMP quark coupling structures
yielding the SI and SD interactions. Second, the SI and SD interactions are expected to
dominate scattering compared to other interactions, since the SI and SD interactions survive
in the limit of vanishing WIMP velocity in contrast to the other interactions. It is therefore
reasonable to expect that the canonical SI and SD interactions dominate WIMP-nucleus
scattering and that other interactions can be safely ignored. A detailed analysis of this
expectation in view of the bottom-up NREFT for WIMP-nucleus scattering is carried out in
this thesis.

In chapter 5, we described the formalism of NREFT, which provides a model-independent
framework for classifying the gamut of WIMP-nucleon interactions. When retaining terms
up to second order, the NREFT generates a total of 14 operators – 2 of which correspond to
the traditional SI and SD interactions. This enlarged set of operators leads to new interactions

i Either solely to account for DM or to address other issues plaguing the SM; it is arguably preferable for a
theory to do the latter!

Chapter 6 Summary and Conclusions

(and corresponding novel nuclear responses), such as angular momentum dependent (LD)
interactions where DM couples to the angular momentum of the nucleus and angular
momentum and spin dependent (LSD) interactions where DM interacts with the spin-orbit
coupling of the nucleus. The NREFT formalism also accommodates improved nuclear
structure calculations of the novel nuclear responses appearing in connection with the new
interactions.

In particular, Ref. [346] advocates for the inclusion of various NREFT operators including
those suppressed by powers of momentum transferii and relative WIMP-nucleon velocity. The
authors of Ref. [346] reason that owing to the lack of knowledge of non-gravitational couplings
of DM to SM particles, assumptions about such couplings motivated from minimalism or
specific electroweak-scale particle physics models may not be suitable. They further argue that
the momentum- or velocity-dependent operators appearing in the NREFT’s enlarged operator
set are well-motivated since the leading, momentum- or velocity-independent interactions can
be easily suppressed or made to vanish, thereby leaving the momentum- or velocity-dependent
interaction as the dominant contributions to scattering. In this thesis, we have scrutinized
these considerations by inspecting the contributions of the sub-leading operators (appearing
at the first order in the NREFT expansion) to WIMP-nucleus scattering.

The NLO operators under consideration include O10, O11 and O12 and are odd under both
Parity (P) and Time Reversal (T) discrete symmetries. These three operators are the only
operators to be odd under both P and T out of the 14 NREFT operators. O10 involves a
product of the 3-momentum transfer with nuclear spin, and hence leads to SD interactionsiii.
O11 involves a product of the 3-momentum transfer with DM spin, and hence leads to SI
interactions. O12 involves both a Galilean invariant product of DM spin, nuclear spin and the
component of WIMP-nucleon velocity transverse to the 3-momentum transfer. Assuming
local and Lorentz invariant QFTs, an invariance under CPT implies that the P-odd, T-odd
NREFT operators must be generated by a CP violating theory. Since there exist stringent
constraints on CP violation in the SM, we used the notion that CP violating observables
can be used to constrain such NREFT operators. The choice of the CP violating observable
herein is the nEDM, which is subject to an extremely strict upper bound.

There have been a number of articles in the literature connecting a variety of well-known
SM extensions to low energy NREFT operators. In this thesis, attention is directed towards
Ref. [359], which identified various simplified models extending the SM with a DM candidate
and a mediator particle; these models altogetheriv give rise to the entire set of NREFT
operators in the low energy limit. It is worth noting that simplified models do not respect

that simplified models contain fewer parameters (as compared to fully SM gauge invariant

We used the simplified models of Ref. [359] which violate CP and reduce to the P-odd, T-odd
O10, O11 and O12 in the NR limit. We derived bound(s) on the WIMP-nucleon scattering
cross section of such operators from the induced nEDM, and compared them to limits from
direct searches. This is the central focus of the articles presented in Appendix A and B.

In the first article [1], we studied two simplified models according to which a DM particle
elastically scatters on SM quarks in s-channel exchanges of charged mediators. Charged here
refers to the mediators carrying 𝑆𝑈 (3)𝐶 color and𝑈 (1)em electric charge. The firstv model
(Model I therein) contained a spin-0 WIMP and one or more heavy quark-like mediators.
The second model (Model II therein) contained a spin-1/2 WIMP and one or more complex
spin-0 mediators.

We highlighted that despite the acclaimed minimal nature of simplified models,𝑈 (1)em
invariance necessitated the introduction of multiple mediators, which then allows the
introduction of many additional parameters. Further, these models result in flavor changing
neutral currents (FCNC) at one-loop order, which are well constrained in the SM. Therefore,
we assumed that each mediator coupled to only one quark type (u-type or d-type), implying a
flavor diagonal structure for the Yukawa coupling matrices.

While the first model gave rise to only 3 operators viz. O1, O7 ad O10, the second model
generated 9 of the 14 NREFT operators including O1, O4, O10, O11 and O12. This is not
surprising since the set of NREFT operators contains fewer operators for spin-0 DM than for
DM with non-zero spin. It is relevant to note that these simplified models were originally
formulated specifically to generate O10 and O11 NREFT operators [359]. Hence, it was
natural to consider if the zeroth order operators O1 and O4 could be easily suppressed or
tuned to zero. We demonstrated that the opposite holds — generally the coefficient of O1
is not easily suppressed in either of the first and the second model, and that arranging the
coefficient of O1 to vanish necessitated two distinct cancellation relations, each holding to
one part in 103 or better. Since direct search experiments altogether involve different targets
with several isotopes, the coefficient of O1 must be suppressed for both neutrons and protons.
Such cancellation conditions are ad-hoc and not motivated by any particle physics principle
such as a symmetry. As a result, we concluded that the contributions from zeroth order
operators will usually dominate and overwhelm those from other operators, at the very least
within the context of the simplified models considered.

Assuming the cancellations relations hold true so that O1 is suppressed, we computed
one-loop contributions to the nEDM which are present in both models. Upon constructing
relativistic effective operators and performing their non-relativistic reduction, we recognized

that, for both models, the Wilson coefficients of the (P-odd) CPVvi NREFT operators and the
nEDM contribution are proportional to the same combination of Yukawa couplings. This
allowed us to derive an indirect bound on the WIMP-nucleon cross sections of the operators
using the upper bound on neutron’s EDM. Therefore, we compared these indirect bounds
with the (then)vii leading limits obtained by direct search experiments. We found that the
derived bounds from the nEDM are several orders of magnitude stronger than the limits from
direct searches for DM masses ranging from sub-GeV to TeV across both models. Further,
the indirect nEDM upper bound on the WIMP-nucleon cross section was found to be far
stronger than the neutrino floor limit — which can be understood as a final sensitivity limit
of direct detection experiments. This implies the following: first, signals of DM-nucleus
scatterings due to such operators would be greatly overwhelmed by the background signals
from neutrino-nucleus scattering: and second, even if, arguendo, the neutrino background
could somehow be ignored or discriminated from DM signals, compliance with the indirect
nEDM bound would result in inordinately small DM scattering event rates. Consequently, we
concluded that these contributions from the NREFT operators are minuscule in comparison
to the traditional SI O1 and SD O4 operators. This conclusion holds true only if the couplings
of the simplified models are not subjected to contrived fine tuning relations to suppress
coefficient of O1 to neutrons and protons as well as the nEDM.

In the second article [2], we considered simplified models with neutral spin-0 mediators
where DM-quark elastic scattering proceeds via t-channel. In contrast to [1], the mediators
are neutral with respect to the 𝑆𝑈 (3)𝐶 color and𝑈 (1)em electric charge(s). In these simplified
models, the leading SI operator O1 is already present at tree-level since couplings which
generate it are permitted by the 𝑆𝑈 (3)𝐶 × 𝑈 (1)em gauge symmetry. Despite this, the
coefficient of O1 can be tuned away by simply setting the relevant coupling(s) to zero. We
emphasized that this is a spurious choice since it is not supported by any underlying symmetry.
Therefore, presumably, these models would generate the P-odd, T-odd operators O10 or O11
while the leading order operator O1 would be absent. It should be noted that there are no
one-loop level contributions to the nEDM anymore since the coupling(s), which at tree-level
give rise to O1, also generating nEDM contributions at one-loop have been “switched” off.

However, since coupling(s) matching on to the SI operator O1 are not expressly forbidden
by the gauge symmetries of the simplified model, the coefficient of O1 would expectedly be
finite at the next order in perturbation theory. Therefore, we computed the coefficient of O1
induced from one-loop box and triangle Feynman diagrams. Owing to loop suppression of

For the third model (Model I in [2]) where O10 arises from tree-level WIMP-quark

loop nEDM upper bound can be circumvented either if the trilinear scalar coupling (trilinear

of the couplings relevant for the nEDM are suitably fine tuned. We highlighted that the
latter option would push the WIMP-nucleon cross sections for both operators O1 and O11
beyond the neutrino floor, thus rendering such WIMP-nucleon interactions insensitive for
direct search experiments. In regard to the former option, we argued that it was another
spurious choice: there is no symmetry which would explain this zero value. Forcing the
trilinear scalar coupling to zero merely suppresses it at the lowest order in perturbation theory.
Unsurprisingly, we found that radiative corrections do indeed induce a non-zero value of the
trilinear self-coupling at one-loop. These radiative corrections mean that the nEDM is then
effectively induced at the three-loop level. Rather than performing the exacting three-loop
computation, we used a lower bound on the trilinear self-coupling from one-loop triangle
diagrams to estimate an indirect lower bound on the nEDM. We found that the obtained
nEDM bound on the WIMP-nucleon cross section is still stronger than limits from direct
search experiments and largely same as or below the neutrino floor. We concluded that it is
essential to consider the nEDM constraint for studying detection prospects of the operator
O10 and that for virtually all cases, the contributions from O10 can be safely neglected.

For the fourth model (Model II in [2]) where the subleading SI operator O11 arises from
tree-level WIMP-quark interactions, we found that loop-induced contributions from O1, in
certain regions of the parameter space, still dominate the subleading O11 contribution. This
only holds true if the trilinear scalar coupling is not suppressed. Interestingly, in contrast to
the models for O10, the CP violation is confined to the dark sector and no stringent constraint
for the nEDM can be obtained. We thus concluded this simplified model constitutes a scenario
where a subleading NREFT operator O11 dominates over the canonical SI operator. We
reiterate that this conclusion rests upon the tree-level coupling(s) for the latter being set to
zero, which is not technically natural. We do remark here that it is not presently clear if a
BSM model where O11 dominates, which is fully SM gauge invariant and leads to detectable
WIMP-nucleon scattering rates, can be constructed.

Overall, both chapters A and B taken together strongly indicate that constraints from the
nEDM cast doubt on the importance of the P-odd, T-odd NREFT operators for analysing

WIMP-nucleus scattering. Our results imply that in most cases, instead of providing standalone
dominating contributions, the subleading P-odd, T-odd operators provide corrections to the
canonical SI operator, which is coherently enhanced.

Although the NREFT with its enlarged set of operators provides a more complete description
of WIMP-nucleus scattering, the NREFT should be viewed as an EFT expansion in powers of
the WIMP velocity. It thus naturally follows that the NLO and NNLO terms of the expansion
are suppressed relative to the LO operators arising from the zeroth order termsviii in the
expansion.

In summary, our results strongly indicate that the canonical SI operator O1 is still the most
important operator. The SI subleading P-odd, T-odd operator O11 can sometimes have the
same relevance as O1 and thus constitutes the second most important operator. In this regard,
the NREFT indeed identifies a WIMP-nucleon interaction which had previously been less
explored in the literature.

6.1 Outlook
The analysis of the subleading P-odd, T-odd operators presented in chapters A and B is by
no means exhaustive. In carrying out the analysis, universal flavor-diagonal couplings of the
mediator to the DM particle and SM quarks (in Article 1) and to the SM quarks (in Article 2)
were assumed. This was chosen to simplify the model building and to avoid constraints from
loop-suppressed FCNC processes within the SM. A next point of inquiry would then concern
relaxing this assumption. The mediator couplings could then be constrained by bounds on
neutral meson mixing processes (for 𝐾 , 𝐷, 𝐵𝑠 and 𝐵𝑑 neutral mesons) and rare meson decays.
It would be interesting to additionally compare constraints from the flavor sector with the
bounds on the leading and subleading NREFT operators.

In this regard, non-trivial flavor structures of the Yukawa couplings involving the mediator
could be explored. The Yukawa couplings could be assumed to increase with increasing
quark massix. This is at least motivated from the flavor structure of SM, where the Yukawa
couplings of the increase with increasing fermion mass. Consequently, in the simplified
models we have considered, the WIMP-nucleon scattering amplitude would be dominated by
contributions from heavy quarks. Thus, the relevant WIMP-quark scattering contributions
would appear at the next order in perturbation theory. This would be at the one-loop level for
the models in Article 1 and at the two-loop level for the models in Article 2. Further, the
contribution to the nEDM would then also be dominated by the heavy quark contributions.
Heavy quarks contribute to the nEDM via the Weinberg three-gluon operator [95], which is a
dimension-six effective operator, and thus the heavy quark contributions to the nEDM appear,

ix We note at least two different scalings of the Yukawa couplings — one in which the couplings scale linearly
