to be weaker owing to the additional loop suppression for the heavy quark contributions.
Therefore, it would be worthwhile to check if the nEDM bound would still be stronger than
limits from direct search experiments for the P-odd, T-odd operators. Overall, these scenarios,
where the heavy quark contributions dominate the light quark contributions to the scattering
amplitude as well as the nEDM, need further scrutiny to bolster the arguments already made
herein.

Another issue which could be examined in more detail is the three-loop estimate of the
nEDM. This estimate was obtained by using a lower bound on the trilinear scalar coupling due
to one-loop corrections. The indirect nEDM constraint on the WIMP-nucleon cross section
for O10 could certainly be improved upon by performing the full three-loop computation.
Although it is expected that the full three-loop computation would provide corrections to the
nEDM estimate obtained here, qualitative changes to the overall results are not anticipated.

It is not clear whether the entirety of the conclusions drawn here for the subleading P-odd,
T-odd NREFT operators would hold true in the framework of UV-complete extensions of the
SM. Naturally, many UV completions of the simplified models discussed herein are possible,
and thus the nEDM constraint would have to be evaluated individually for a specific UV
completion. For instance, identifying the scalar mediator in the third and the fourth models
to be the SM Higgs results would force its couplings to the SM quarks to be small and equip
the WIMP with additional gauge interactions. These additional gauge interactions would
then subject to a variety of constraints. Therefore, further investigation of constraints based
on nEDM on NREFT operators in UV complete theories is needed.

Chiral contributions to WIMP-nucleus scattering, where WIMP couples to the virtual
mesons (e.g. the light 𝜋, 𝜂 mesons), exchanged between two nucleons bound in the nucleus,
can be sizable [352–356]. Such contributions provide two-body nucleonic corrections for one-
body nucleonic NREFT operators. In some cases, the corrections from chiral contributions
can overcome the momentum transfer suppression of certain NREFT operators. Such chiral
contributions have been organized using a chiral perturbation theory EFT for WIMP-nucleus
scattering [360, 361]. It would be interesting to study if chiral corrections can possibly affect
the hierarchy among the NLO and NNLO NREFT operators generated in the simplified
models considered here. In particular, chiral corrections to O11 in the fourth model may be
important and could render it dominant over O1 also for large DM masses.

The analysis in this thesis has been restricted to spin-0 and spin-1/2 DM particles. Naturally,
simplified models for spin-1 could be considered and it would then be interesting to see the
interplay of constraints from nEDM with the complexity of model building required to obtain
viable vector DM candidates.

To conclude, it is hoped that the analysis carried out in this thesis can be of relevance not
just for the remainder of the future of direct searches but also for the wider pursuit of pinning
down particle properties of DM.

A non-relativistic effective field theory (NREFT) offers a bottom-up framework to classify Dark Matter 
(DM) – nucleon interactions relevant for scattering at direct detection experiments by organizing the 
interactions in powers of the momentum transfer �q and DM velocity �v . This approach generates a number 
of operators including P-odd and T-odd operators; these can only be generated from a relativistic theory 
with CP violating interactions. We consider the leading order P-odd, T-odd operators viz. O10, O11 and 
O12 and compare the constraints on these operators from leading direct detection searches and from 
the bound on the neutron EDM (nEDM). We perform our analysis using simplified models with charged 
mediators and compute the loop diagrams contributing to the nEDM. We find that constraints on the 
DM scattering cross section from the bound on the nEDM are several orders of magnitude stronger than 
the limits from direct searches, and even well below the neutrino floor for such NREFT operators, for the 
entire sub-GeV to TeV DM mass range. We conclude that one may not need to consider these operators 
when analyzing data from present or future direct dark matter detection experiments.

1. Introduction

The particle identity of Dark Matter (DM) has not yet been 
understood despite overwhelming evidence for its gravitational 
interactions. Dedicated direct searches exploit the possible non-
gravitational interactions of DM by looking for the recoil of target 
nuclei due to elastic scattering and have already probed a large 
fraction of DM mass and cross-section parameter space [1–10].

Much of the direct detection search strategy for roughly three 
decades has been focused on a category of DM candidates known 
as Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs). WIMPs with 
weak-scale masses, produced in the early universe via freeze-out 
from the thermal plasma [11], can easily match the measured 
DM relic abundance via roughly electroweak-strength couplings to 
Standard Model (SM) particles. Most analyses assume DM-nucleon 
interactions to be dominated by only two operators, which de-
scribe Spin-Independent (SI) or Spin-Dependent (SD) interactions 
in the limit of vanishing WIMP velocity. The leading bounds on 
SI DM-nucleon cross section and SD DM-neutron cross section are 
currently set by XENON1T [1,3]; for a 30 GeV WIMP, the bounds 
are 4.1 × 10−47 cm2 and 6.3 × 10−42 cm2, respectively. The best di-
rect detection bound on the SD DM-proton cross section comes

The NREFT contains a total of 28 free parameters if operators

or velocity suppressed operators that are odd under P (parity) and

both theorists and experimenters. This motivates analyses of parti-

in the non-relativistic limit.

From a particle physics perspective, the CPT theorem implies 
that all P- and T-odd NREFT operators must necessarily arise from 
a CP violating theory, where C refers to charge conjugation. How-
ever, CP violation (CPV) is highly constrained experimentally [29]
and therefore bounds on CPV observables can be used to constrain 
such NREFT operators. The neutron EDM (nEDM) is one such ob-
servable which probes flavor diagonal CP violation and provides 
one of the most stringent bounds on CPV in extensions of the 
SM. Ongoing nEDM experiments are sensitive to a possible signal 
which is many orders of magnitude larger than the SM prediction 
[29,30]. The current constraint is

|dn| < 2.9 × 10−26 e · cm (90 % C.L.) . (1)

Various works have linked well-motivated extensions of the SM 
to low energy NREFT operators [31–35]. In particular, Ref. [36] lists 
a set of simplified models for scalar, spinor and vector DM can-
didates and derives the full set of NREFT operators in terms of 
the parameters for each simplified model. In this letter, we inves-
tigate the P- and T-odd operators in the NREFT with the help of 
simplified models that respect SU (3) × U (1)em invariance and are 
renormalizable, as in [36]. The models in this work extend the SM 
by a WIMP candidate and a charged mediator particle. We show 
that in these models the Wilson coefficients of the CPV NREFT op-
erators and of the neutron EDM scale with the same combination 
of Yukawa couplings. As a result, we find that the constraints from 
the nEDM on the scattering cross section are many orders of mag-
nitude stronger for both CPV NREFT operators than the current 
XENON1T bound and even lie below the irreducible background 
from coherent neutrino scattering (“neutrino floor”) [37–40]. This 
expresses doubt about the importance of these operators for the 
analysis of future experiments [41].

The rest of this letter is organized as follows. In Section 2 we 
introduce the NREFT formalism, the matching procedure of a rela-
tivistic theory to NREFT operators and review the computation of 
the differential event rate for elastic WIMP-nucleus scattering. In 
Section 3 we consider two simplified models yielding these P- and 
T-odd CPV NREFT operators and compute the nEDM at 1-loop or-
der for each case. Section 4 contains our main numerical results, 
comparing the nEDM and the leading direct detection bound. We 
conclude in Section 5.

3. DM simplified models

Simplified models of DM provide a minimal framework to ex-
plore its phenomenology across direct, indirect and LHC searches. 
In these models the SM is augmented with a WIMP candidate 
and a mediator via which quarks and/or leptons can interact with 
WIMPs. Although renormalizable and invariant under SU (3)C ×
U (1)em gauge transformations, they usually ignore the SU (2) part 
of the SM gauge group; they are therefore not UV complete the-
ories. However, since simplified models contain a relatively small 
number of parameters they can be powerful tools to interpret ex-
perimental results and explore the complementarity of different 
searches.

Ref. [36] has constructed a set of simplified models by ex-
haustively listing different WIMP and mediator spins and matched 
the resulting relativistic Lagrangians to the set of non-relativistic 
operators listed in Table 1. In these models the WIMP is an 
SU (3)C × U (1)em singlet; the interactions are further constrained 
by the requirement that the WIMP cannot decay.

Here we focus on two simplified models with color-triplet me-
diators which in the NR limit give rise to the leading order P- and 
T-odd operators O11, O10 and O12; O11 is spin-independent while 
O10 and O12 are spin dependent. In the following subsections we 
describe these models and use the experimental upper bound on 
the neutron EDM to constrain their direct detection prospects.

4. Results and discussion

We had seen in the previous Section that the same combina-
tion of Yukawa couplings appears in the expression of the nEDM 
and in the coefficients of the P- and T-odd operators contributing

with the most recent XENON1T results [1] as well as with the ir-
reducible “neutrino floor” background in Xenon experiments.

5. Conclusions

We studied the detection prospects of P- and T-odd operators 
arising in the NREFT formalism for WIMP-nucleus elastic scatter-
ing. These operators occur only if one includes terms that are sup-
pressed by powers of relative velocity or three-momentum trans-
fer. They can therefore be expected to be significant only if the 

coefficient of the leading spin-independent operator O1 is very 
small or vanishes. Moreover, T-odd NREFT operators can only arise 
in the low-energy limit of a relativistic theory if the latter violates 
CP invariance. This can give rise to very stringent constraints on 
the theory, in particular from electric dipole moments.

We analyzed these issues in the framework of two simpli-
fied models, taken from ref. [36]. They introduce one or more 
s-channel mediator(s) carrying electric and color charge, with spin 
1/2 (Model I) or 0 (Model II); the dark matter particle then has 
spin 0 or 1/2, respectively. These models will cause FCNC at one-
loop unless each mediator only couples to one quark. Moreover, 
we pointed out that generically the coefficient of O1 is not sup-
pressed in these models. Since by now strong constraints on spin-
independent WIMP-nucleon scattering exist for several isotopes, 
the new operators will be significant only if the coefficient of O1 is 
suppressed for both neutrons and protons. This generically requires 
two independent cancellations, which should hold to one part in 
103 or better. We also note that one has to introduce several me-
diators for these cancellations to be possible at all, i.e. in minimal 
versions of these models, with a single mediator, the contribution 
from O1 will always dominate.

We therefore assumed that the new couplings and mediator 
masses are universal for all generations. Since in this case the 
new terms in the Lagrangian respect strong isospin invariance the 
two cancellation conditions become almost the same. However, we 
showed that these scenarios give rise to one-loop contributions 
to the electric dipole moment of the neutron (nEDM) which are 
proportional to exactly the same combination of new Yukawa cou-
plings which appears in the coefficients of the new P- and T-odd 
NREFT operators. The resulting indirect constraint lies well below 
the irreducible neutrino background. This implies that the con-
tributions from the new T-odd operators on the WIMP-nucleon 
scattering can safely be neglected in the analyses of both current 
and future experiments. This conclusion can only be avoided if 
one relaxes the universality assumption on the new couplings and 
mediator masses. However, one will then have to impose three in-
dependent conditions, in order to cancel the coefficients of O1 for 
protons and neutrons as well as the neutron EDM. Since these can-
cellations are not enforced by any symmetry, we conclude that it is 
very unlikely indeed that the new T-odd operators can contribute 
significantly. We emphasize that, for a given size of the Wilson co-
efficients, these are the most important of the total eleven new 
operators. This indicates that at least in models with charged me-
diator coupling to light quarks, WIMP-nucleon scattering can safely 
be analyzed using the traditional operators O1 and O4 only.

Constraints from the neutron EDM on subleading
effective operators for direct Dark Matter searches

Manuel Drees and Rahul Mehra ∗

Bethe Center for Theoretical Physics and Physikalisches Institut, Universität Bonn,
Nussallee 12, D-53115 Bonn, Germany

E-mail: drees@th.physik.uni-bonn.de, rmehra@physik.uni-bonn.de

Abstract: Interactions between Dark Matter (DM) and nucleons relevant for direct search
experiments can be organised in a model independent manner using a Galiliean invariant,
non-relativistic effective field theory (NREFT). Here one expands the interactions in powers
of the momentum transfer q⃗ and DM velocity v⃗. This approach generates many operators.
The potentially most important subleading operators are odd under T , and can thus only
be present in a theory with CP violating interactions. We consider two such operators,
called O10 and O11 in the literature, in simplified models with neutral spin−0 mediators; the
couplings are chosen such that the coefficient of the leading spin independent (SI) operator,
which survives for v⃗ → 0, vanishes at tree level. However, it is generically induced at the
next order in perturbation theory. We perform a numerical comparison of the number of
scattering events between interactions involving the T−odd operators and the corresponding
loop induced SI contributions. We find that for “maximal” CP violation the former can
dominate over the latter. However, in two of the three models we consider, an electric dipole
moment of the neutron (nEDM) is induced at two-loop order. We find that the experimental
bound on the nEDM typically leads to undetectably small rates induced by O10. On the
other hand, the model leading to a nonvanishing coefficient of O11 does not induce an nEDM.

Keywords: CP Violation, Electric Dipole Moments, Models for Dark Matter, Particle
Nature of Dark Matter

1 Introduction

The search for non-gravitational interactions of Dark Matter (DM) has not yielded a convincing
signal so far. This is in stark contrast with the accumulated evidence for its gravitational
interactions across a broad range of astrophysical length scales. Direct searches aim to detect
non-gravitational interactions by observing the recoil of a target nucleus after an incoming
DM particle has scattered off it. Terrestrial experiments using this search principle have led to
tight constraints on the DM mass and cross-section parameter space [1–14]. For the past few
decades such experimental efforts have focused on particle DM with weak scale interactions
termed as Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs). WIMPs can be produced in the
early universe through freeze-out from the thermal plasma, which yields the observed DM
relic abundance [15] for very roughly electroweak strength effective couplings. This has made
WIMPs a particularly compelling category of DM candidates.

In order to interpret the results of direct search experiments one has to make assumptions
regarding the nature of the interaction between DM and nucleons. Traditionally it was
assumed that DM-nucleon interactions are dominated by just two operators describing spin
independent (SI) and spin dependent (SD) interactions in the limit of zero WIMP velocity [16].
These SI and SD operators are the leading terms of an EFT description, which is an expansion
in powers of small parameters such as the DM velocity v and three momentum transfer
scaled by the nucleon mass q⃗/mN . Since v/c ≲ O(10−3) in the solar neighborhood, the
momentum transfer is restricted to |q⃗| ≲ O(100MeV). Although the momentum exchange
can be substantial on nuclear physics scales, it is far below the electroweak scale, and also
below the range of WIMP masses most direct search experiments can probe. Hence, it is

reasonable to expect that the canonical SI and SD interactions (zeroth order terms) dominate

A detailed non-relativistic effective field theory (NREFT) description of elastic DM-
nucleus scattering retains NLO and NNLO terms by modeling the nucleus as a spatially
extended composite particle with spin and charge densities [17–20]. For WIMPs of spins 0
or 1/2, truncating the EFT expansion at second order generates a total of 14 operators.1
Since these higher order terms vanish for v → 0 (which implies q⃗ → 0 as well), they lead to
a spectrum of recoil energies quite different from the usual quasi-exponential fall-off, often
preferring energies larger than the typical range of values implemented for SI and SD searches
in experiments [23]. Multiple experiments have now extended their recoil energy search
window in order to optimize the search strategy in the NREFT framework [24–33].

The NREFT contains, at least, 28 free parameters when the operators for neutrons
and protons are counted separately. Probing this large parameter space is an arduous
task. A number of global analyses using data from current and planned direct detection
experiments have placed upper limits on the coupling strengths in this multi-dimensional
parameter space [34–41]. A common conclusion drawn from these global analyses is that
experiments are nearly as sensitive to some momentum– or velocity-dependent operators
that are odd under P (parity) and T (time reversal) transformations as they are to the
leading SD operator. These subleading operators have been scrutinized less in the literature.
It is therefore interesting to study the phenomenology of models where they are generated
in the non-relativistic (NR) limit, and to understand when these operators can dominate
over the traditional SI and SD interactions.

The CPT theorem [42, 43] implies that every T−odd NREFT operator must arise from a
CP−violating (CPV) quantum field theory, where C refers to charge conjugation. However,
there are extremely stringent experimental constraints on CP violation [44], which can be
used to place constraints on such NREFT operators. The electric dipole moment of the
neutron (nEDM) is one such observable. The sensitivity of current experiments [45–47] is
several orders of magnitude above the prediction of the standard model of particle physics
(SM), but they provide tight constraints on flavor diagonal CP violation in extensions of
the SM. The experimental upper limit on the nEDM is

|dn| < 1.8× 10−26 e · cm (90 % C.L.). (1.1)

There have been a number of articles linking extensions of the SM to low energy NREFT
operators [48–50]. In particular, ref. [48] lists a set of simplified models for scalar, spinorial
and vector DM candidates and derives the full set of NREFT operators in terms of the
parameters for each simplified model. However, it is worth noting that most extensions of
the SM only generate a small subset of the NREFT operators. Moreover, in most cases
the leading order operators describing the SI and SD interactions are generated as well,
and will then typically dominate. However, it is conceivable that the standard operators
are strongly suppressed, in which case formally subleading operators actually provide the
dominant contribution to scattering.

In ref. [51], we considered simplified models with charged mediators, which are exchanged
in the s−channel in DM-nucleon scattering. We found that suppressing the leading SI operator
required finetuning of couplings; moreover, the bound on the nEDM, which is generated at
one-loop in these models, implies that the subleading operators lead to undetectably small
DM scattering rates. The P−odd, T−odd operators can thus be neglected in such scenarios.

In this article, we consider models that augment the SM by a WIMP candidate and
a mediator particle which does not carry electric or color charge; DM-nucleon scattering
then proceeds via t−channel diagrams. We focus on WIMPs with spin 0 or 1/2, since in a
renormalizable theory a spin−1 boson needs to be a gauge boson, making the construction of
(semi-)realistic models somewhat more cumbersome. If one allows all couplings that respect
the SU(3)C × U(1)em gauge symmetry of the simplified Lagrangian, the leading SI term will
be generated at tree level. However, the coefficient of this operator can be “switched off” by
setting relevant coupling(s) to zero. This is an ad hoc choice, which cannot be justified by
any symmetry. In this case, at the lowest order in perturbation theory, these models generate
the P−odd, T−odd operators O10 or O11 without giving rise to the leading order operators.

However, since the vanishing of the coefficient of the leading SI operator is not enforced
by a symmetry, it will usually be generated at the next order in perturbation theory. Since
now the contribution from the leading operator to DM-nucleon scattering is loop suppressed2

while the contributions from O10 and O11 are suppressed by powers of v or |q⃗|/mN , it is not
a priori obvious which contribution is more important. We therefore numerically compare
these contributions to the total number of events for a Xenon target. We find that for large
regions in the parameter space of these models, the subleading P−odd, T−odd operators
actually dominate over the SI term if the latter is purely loop-induced.

However, in models where tree level interactions generate only O10, we find that an
nEDM is generically induced at two-loop order. The resulting upper bound on the couplings
then again leads to unobservably small scattering rates, so that contributions from O10 to
DM-nucleon scattering can be neglected. On the other hand, in the model where O11 is
generated at tree level, the CP violation is restricted to the dark sector, and no nEDM is
generated (apart from the tiny SM contribution). This case then provides an example of
an NLO operator dominating over the traditional SI operator in DM-nucleon scattering,
at least at the level of a simplified model.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. In section 2, we provide a brief
introduction to the NREFT formalism, and introduce three CP violating simplified models
yielding the P− and T−odd NREFT operators. We also compute the loop diagrams for
WIMP-nucleon scattering that give rise to the leading SI operator in the non-relativistic
limit. We then match the different scattering contributions to the corresponding four-
field effective operators and finally match these to the set of NREFT operators. We also
compute the two-loop Feynman diagrams that induce a nEDM and discuss the implications
for the corresponding P−, T−odd operator in the NREFT. In section 3 we compute the

2 NREFT and simplified models

A non-relativistic effective field theory (NREFT) of elastic scattering between DM and
nuclei exhaustively categorizes the possible interactions involved in direct searches. An
incoming DM particle striking a target nucleus on Earth is quite slow in the detector rest
frame, v/c ∼ O(10−3), and therefore a non-relativistic EFT can be used to describe the
scattering. This simplifies the nuclear physics required to compute the scattering rate,
which is nevertheless rather nontrivial [18]. Traditionally only the leading terms were kept,
which remain finite as v → 0 [16]. The first and second order terms in DM velocity v and
momentum transfer q⃗/mN (in units of the nucleon mass) were considered only relatively

Connecting a relativistic model for DM leading to specific DM-quark and/or DM-gluon
interactions with the NREFT in general involves two steps. First, one integrates out the
heavy mediator(s), where “heavy” here refers to all mediators ϕ with mass mϕ well above
100MeV, which is the maximal three-momentum exchange in DM-nucleus scattering.4 This
results in relativistic but non-renormalizable four-field DM-quark and/or DM-gluon operators.
In the second step one takes the non-relativistic limit of these four-field operators and matches
them onto the NREFT operators listed in table 1. This leads to an effective Lagrangian
containing some (or all) of these operators, with coefficients determined by the couplings and
masses of the original relativistic theory. The computation of DM-nucleus scattering rates
from these coefficients involves numerous nuclear “response functions”; we refer to ref. [20],
whose expressions we used in our own numerical code.

As already mentioned, the NREFT is an expansion in powers of v or q⃗. If all coefficients
in the NREFT are of comparable magnitude, the total scattering rate typically receives
the largest contribution from the SI operator O1, which is of zeroth order in the expansion.
Moreover, this contribution is enhanced by A2, where A is the nucleon number. For large
momentum exchange, |q⃗| ≳ 1/rN where rN is the radius of the target nucleus, the rate is
somewhat suppressed by a form factor, but even without form factor this contribution to
the scattering rate peaks at |q⃗| → 0.
O4 is also of zeroth order in the expansion. However, since the spins of the nucleons largely

cancel in any given nucleus, there is no A2 enhancement; in fact, O4 does not contribute
at all if the target nucleus has no spin.

As already noted, for sufficiently heavy DM particle (and target nucleus) the three-
momentum exchange can reach |q⃗| ∼ 100MeV. In this high momentum exchange region
of phase space the operators that are linear in q⃗ and independent of v⃗⊥ are therefore only
suppressed by a factor ∼ 0.1; these are the operators O10 and O11 which are the focus of
our study.5 The contribution from O11 is A2 enhanced, up to a form factor, but requires
the DM particle to carry spin. The contribution from O10 suffers similar cancellations as
that from O4, but can survive even for scalar DM particle.

Naively the contributions of operators involving v⃗⊥ should be suppressed by a factor
v2 ∼ 10−6; indeed, compared to the contribution from O1 this is almost true. However, the
richer structures can lead to nuclear response ∝ S⃗N · L⃗N [20], L⃗N being the orbital angular
momentum of a given nucleon; in this product the contributions of paired nucleons do not
cancel. As a result, for heavy target nuclei and similar coefficients the contribution from O12
often exceeds that from O4 [39]; however, as already noted O12 is not generated in the models
with neutral mediator that we consider in this article. Similarly, for equal coefficients O3
typically contributes almost as much as O10 does [39], but O3 is not generated in leading order
when starting from a relativistic theory [48]. O10 and O11 are therefore the potentially most
important higher order NREFT operators that can be generated from a relativistic QFT.

After these preliminaries, we are ready to introduce the simplified models we consider
in this analysis. Recall that, in the spirit of ref. [48], we only impose invariance under
SU(3)C × U(1)em, not under the complete gauge group of the SM.

and a mediator ϕ in the loop is concerned, the mediator can consistently be defined as being
CP−even, since only the coupling hq1 appears in the diagram. Similarly, in Model I and
Model IIa, in the one-loop diagram with a quark-mediator loop the mediator can consistently
be defined as being CP−odd, since only the coupling hq2 appears.

Turning to higher loops, a CP−even mediator can have any self coupling. Hence in
Model IIb embellishing the one-loop diagram with additional scalar vertices does not lead to
CP violation. In fact, in this model the only coupling that is not consistent with interpreting
ϕ to be CP−even is λ2, which couples ϕ to the DM particle. However, this coupling cannot
contribute to electric dipole moments. It could appear in any diagram where the only external
particles are a through-going quark and a photon (or gluon) only via a closed χ loop, which
will either vanish (if an odd number of ϕ legs is attached to it), or simply renormalize a
CP−even quantity like the ϕ 2−point function. We thus conclude that in Model IIb, no new
contributions to the electric dipole moments of SM particles are generated. The conceptually
easiest way to prove the existence of CP violation in this model is via χq scattering; in case of
2→ 2 scattering, spin observables would have to be included in the construction of a CP−odd
quantity. While conceptually straightforward, experimentally this seems prohibitively difficult;
certainly there are no current experimental constraints from such experiments.

The situation is very different in Models I and IIa, where in the relevant one-loop
diagram the mediator behaves like a pseudoscalar. The reason is that a pseudoscalar cannot
have a ϕ3 coupling. Hence, two-loop diagrams containing both the (pseudoscalar) Yukawa

3 Results and discussions

In the previous section, we described the different contributions to DM-nucleus scattering in
Models I, IIa and IIb. These simplified models were designed such there are no tree-level
contributions to the NREFT operator O1; instead, at tree-level only the P− and T−odd
operators O10 (in Model I and IIa) or O11 (in Model IIb) were generated. Recall that O1
often gives the dominant contribution to DM-nucleus scattering: it appears in leading order
in the NREFT expansion, and its contribution is coherently enhanced by A2 if cn1 ≃ cp1, where
cn1 and cp1 are the Wilson coefficients accompanying O1 for neutron and proton respectively.
However, in the models considered here, O1 arises from box and triangle diagrams appearing
at next-to-leading order in perturbation theory. Therefore, it is not obvious a priori which
operator provides the dominant contribution to DM-nucleus scattering.

absolute numerical error reported by the routine is around O(10−8) for the two values of
the mediator mass mϕ we consider.

4 Summary and conclusions

In this paper we explored the detection prospects involving P− and T−odd operators arising
in the NREFT formalism of WIMP-nucleon scattering. These operators appear at next-to-
leading order in an expansion in WIMP velocity v and momentum transfer q⃗. Since these
quantities accompanying the P− and T−odd operators are quite small, these operators are
expected to be insignificant relative to the leading order operators if the corresponding
Wilson coefficients are of similar magnitude. Hence the additional operators can make
significant contributions only when the coefficient of the leading spin-independent operator O1
is strongly suppressed or vanishes entirely. This typically requires ad hoc choices of couplings in
a relativistic QFT, i.e. one can generally not find a symmetry that suppresses the contribution
from O1 without also suppressing the Wilson coefficients of the additional operators.

Crucially, the P− and T−odd NREFT operators can only occur in the low energy limit
of a QFT that violates the CP symmetry. This can lead to stringent constraints on the
theory, in particular from electric dipole moments.

We addressed these concerns in the framework of three simplified models with uncharged
t−channel mediators, taken from ref. [48]. These models extend the SM by a real scalar
mediator particle ϕ which does not carry electric or color charge, and a DM particle which
has spin 0 (Model I) or spin 1/2 (Model IIa and IIb). These models can generate flavor
changing neutral currents already at tree-level unless the Yukawa couplings of the mediator
are diagonal in the quark mass basis. This can easily be ensured if these new couplings are
flavor-universal, which we therefore assumed in our numerical examples.

The couplings in these models are chosen such that at the lowest order in perturbation
theory, only the P− and T−odd operators O10 and O11 arise in the non-relativistic limit. In
particular, ϕ must not have scalar couplings to both quarks and the DM particle. In Models
I and IIa, the quark couplings are pseudoscalar while the DM couplings are scalar, while in
Model IIb the quark couplings are scalar but the DM couplings are pseudoscalar. Note that
there is no symmetry that forbids scalar quark couplings in Models I and IIa, or scalar DM
couplings in Model IIb. It is therefore not surprising that at the next order in perturbation
theory, one-loop box and triangle diagrams do induce the canonical SI interactions described
by the operator O1 in these models. We compared the tree-level interactions giving rise to
O10 or O11 with the one-loop suppressed interactions yielding O1. To that end we computed
the total number of events due to the two types of interactions for a Xenon target.

In the case of Model I and Model IIa and assuming large couplings in order to generate
detectable event rates, we found that the contributions from O10 can be roughly comparable
to those from O1 for mediator mass mϕ = 125GeV, but for heavier mediator the contributions
from O10 clearly dominates. It thus appears as if O10 could indeed be the most relevant
NREFT operator in these models.

However, we pointed out that the quark-mediator interactions in both models produce
two-loop contributions to dn, the electric dipole moment of the neutron (nEDM). These
contributions scale linearly with the cubic self-interaction of the mediator µ1. For parameter
choices that lead to detectable event rates from O10 and µ1 of order unity (in units of mϕ),
the predicted dn is several orders of magnitude larger than the upper limit reported by
experiments. Even if we set µ1 = 0, non-vanishing trilinear self-interactions are generated

at one-loop level by couplings that also appear in the Wilson coefficient of O10. Estimating
a lower bound on µ1 from these loop diagrams, we find that the resulting upper bound on
the WIMP-nucleus scattering rate is still well below current sensitivity, and often even below
the irreducible background (“neutrino floor”), especially for large mϕ where O10 potentially
dominates the scattering rate. As in case of models with charged, s−channel mediator, where
dn is generated already at one-loop level [51], it is thus essential to consider the dn constraint
when considering prospects for detecting WIMP-nucleus scattering due to O10. We expect
this result to hold true for a simplified model containing a spin−1 WIMP and a neutral
spin−0 mediator with pseudoscalar coupling to quarks, which would also give rise to O10.
Since the WIMP-mediator coupling is again CP-even, electric dipole moments for quarks
will be induced radiatively as well in this case.

In Model IIb, which generates the spin-independent NREFT operator O11, we again found
that the loop-induced contributions from O1 can be larger than the tree-level contribution
due to O11, if the trilinear scalar coupling µ1 is not suppressed. We emphasized that in
this model quark loops generate a logarithmically divergent one-loop contribution to µ1. For
µ1 = 1, O1 typically dominates for large DM masses, while O11 is dominant for small masses,
the cross-over point depending on the values of the other parameters. In this model no new
contributions to dn are generated, and therefore this operator is not subject to the stringent
constraints of the neutron EDM, even though it is also P− and T−odd. At least at the level
of a simplified model one can therefore engineer a scenario where the non-leading operator
O11 dominates the WIMP-nucleon scattering rate.

However, it is by no means clear whether this remains true in the framework of UV-
complete theories. Recall that we only require our Lagrangians to be invariant under
SU(3)C × U(1)em; we did not enforce invariance under the electroweak gauge symmetry.
In particular, the ϕq̄q couplings are not SU(2) × U(1)Y invariant if ϕ is a singlet. The
simplest choice would be to identify ϕ with the Higgs boson of the SM, which resides in a
doublet of SU(2). However, the ϕq̄q couplings are then known to be very small. Moreover,
the WIMP can then also not be a gauge singlet, and would thus have additional (gauge)
interactions leading to additional constraints as well as new contributions to WIMP-nucleon
scattering. Alternatively one can couple a singlet WIMP to a singlet scalar which mixes with
the SM Higgs boson; however, in such a scenario the WIMP-nucleon scattering rate would be
suppressed even further by the mediator-Higgs mixing angle, which has to be rather small in
order not to distort the properties of the physical 125GeV particle too much.

We remind the reader that we assumed universal flavor-diagonal couplings of the mediator
to the quarks. This simplifies the model building, since these couplings are then flavor-diagonal
in any basis. On the other hand, it might appear more natural to assume that the new
couplings increase with increasing quark mass, just as the Yukawa couplings of the SM do.
In this case tree-level FCNC are avoided if the matrices of new Yukawa couplings commute
with the Yukawa coupling matrices of the SM; from the model building point of view it is
not clear why this should be the case. Moreover, keeping the couplings to the top quark
≲ 1 would then require very small couplings to the first generation. In such a scenario
the contributions from heavy quarks might well dominate the DM scattering cross section,
as well as — in Models I and IIa — the electric dipole moment of the neutron. In order

In summary, the results presented in this paper as well as ref. [51] strongly indicate
that the current experimental upper bound on the electric dipole moment of the neutron
excludes the possibility that the operator O10 can make contributions to WIMP-nucleus
scattering to which current or near-future experiments are sensitive. While no such strong
statement can be made for the operator O11 generated by the exchange of a neutral mediator
in the t−channel, it is currently unclear whether such a model can be constructed that
respects the full gauge symmetry of the SM and leads to detectable WIMP-nucleon scattering
being dominated by O11.

(Physics)

i

A search for dark matter recoiling from the Standard
Model Higgs boson using the CMS experiment

Shivani Sanjay Lomte

Abstract

Astrophysical evidence supports the existence of dark matter based on its gravitational
interaction. Astrophysical evidence also suggests that dark matter interacts at most very
weakly with the Standard Model particles. The only purely weakly interacting particles
in the Standard Model are neutrinos, which are too light to account for the observed
energy density of dark matter in the Universe. Therefore, there is compelling motivation
for physics beyond the Standard Model which contains weakly interacting massive par-
ticles. Many beyond the Standard Model theories predict the existence of dark matter
particle candidates that can be produced and detected at high energy colliders, driving
experimental searches at the CERN LHC.

This thesis presents a search for dark matter particles produced in association with a
Higgs boson in proton-proton collisions at

√
s = 13 TeV. The data, collected with the CMS

detector at the LHC, correspond to an integrated luminosity of 101 fb−1. Higgs decay to
a bottom quark-antiquark pair is reconstructed to identify events of interest. The analysis
is performed in exclusive categories targeting both Lorentz-boosted (merged) and resolved
b-pair topologies, covering a wide range of Higgs boson transverse momentum. This
analysis looks for statistically significant deviations from the Standard Model predictions,
either enhancements in specific kinematic regions or a bump in the b-pair invariant mass
distribution. The observed data agree with the Standard Model background predictions.
Constraints are placed on dark matter models predicting new particles or interactions,
such as those in the simplified frameworks of baryonic-Z ′ and 2HDM+a. A statistical
combination is made with a previous search using data collected in 2016 and corresponding
to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb−1. Upper limits at 95% confidence level are set on
the production cross section for these models. These results improve upon the previously
existing LHC limits owing to the larger integrated luminosity and improved identification
of h → bb̄ decay. Potential improvements from an ongoing CMS search using the Run-3
data are discussed, along with the future prospects at a high energy muon collider.



ii

Dedication

This thesis is dedicated to my family.



iii

Acknowledgments

I am thankful to many people who helped me throughout my doctoral journey. First and
foremost, I would like to express my deepest gratitude to my advisor, Professor Sridhara
Dasu. His mentorship has shaped the way I approach research problems, teaching me not
just how to do physics, but also how to think through it carefully and communicate it
clearly. He encouraged me to present at conferences, take on roles within the collaboration,
and pursue work beyond the immediate scope of my dissertation, including contributions
to muon collider studies, all of which helped me develop a broader perspective in the field.
He understood that research has a learning curve, and struck the right balance between
pushing me forward and giving me the space to find my footing. During difficult stretches
of the PhD, his support made a real difference. I am genuinely grateful for his investment
in my growth, and for the researcher I have become under his guidance.

I am also extremely grateful to the other faculty in the UW CMS group, Professors
Kevin Black, Tulika Bose, and Matthew Herndon, for the many insightful discussions
over the years which shaped my understanding of the field, and for creating a research
environment in which students genuinely felt supported and encouraged to grow.

I would also like to thank my undergraduate advisor, Professor Seema Sharma at
IISER Pune, who first set me on this path. Her high standards and insistence on hard
work and rigor shaped the way I approach research, and I carry her lessons with me still.

My sincere thanks go to my dissertation committee members, Professors Kevin Black,
Lisa Everett, and Melinda Soares-Furtado, for taking the time to read this thesis and for
providing thoughtful feedback.

A very special thank you goes to Dr. Varun Sharma, whose mentorship was instru-
mental to this work. Working closely with him taught me how to do physics within CMS
in the most practical sense, from the intricacies of the analysis to understanding the de-
tector and the operations work. He pushed me to keep going when progress was slow, and
offered encouragement at exactly the moments it was needed. I am deeply grateful for his
patience, his rigor, and for the enormous amount I learned under his guidance. Also, a
big thank you to Dr. Bhawna Gomber for her insights and assistance with the analysis.

To the other scientists in the group - Abdollah, Cecile, Charis, Deborah, and Sascha,
thank you for your generosity with your time and knowledge, for helping students navigate
the labyrinth of the CMS world, and for fostering a collaborative atmosphere. I am also
grateful to the computing team - Ajit, Carl, Chad and Dan, for their technical support
and for keeping the systems running smoothly, work that often goes unnoticed but without
which this analysis would have been impossible.

To my fellow graduate students in the CMS group - Susmita, Anagha, Abby, and
Ganesh, thank you for making this journey what it was. When I first arrived at CERN,



iv

you helped me find my footing in a new place, and from that point on, you were there
for all of it, the rewarding moments, going through difficult patches, and everything in
between. The movie nights were, of course, essential. Your friendship meant more than I
can easily put in words and I will always cherish the memories we built. A big thank you
to Wren, Dylan, and Abhishikth for the many stimulating physics discussions, I learned
a great deal from those conversations. And to Ryan and Mitanshu - working through
problems together, and occasionally being the one with the answers, was one of the most
rewarding parts of this PhD.

My time at CERN was made richer by the friends I made there from across the col-
laboration - Alpana, Nukul, Vinay, Bisnupriya, Piyush, Neha, and Amruta. Thank you
for the good conversations, and for making Geneva feel more like home. To my physics
cohort - Avani, Winnie, Anna, Nidhi, and Lekshmi, and to my friends outside of physics -
Feba, Renu, Athira, and Uday - thank you for reminding me that there is a life beyond the
analysis. Your friendship kept me grounded, and I am grateful to have you in my corner.

Finally, I am profoundly grateful to my family - mom, dad, my brother Amey, and
my uncle Balaji. Their unconditional support, patience, and encouragement has been a
constant source of strength, and this achievement could not be possible without them.

Chapter 1

Introduction

Humanity has long sought to understand the fundamental laws that govern the world

around us. Over centuries, this pursuit has transformed from simple observations to a

deeply mathematical and experimentally verified description of nature. Our understanding

has evolved in remarkable ways: the unification of electricity and magnetism into Maxwell’s

electromagnetic theory, the development of quantum mechanics to describe the microscopic

world, and later the formulation of quantum field theory as the language of modern physics

all represent major milestones in this journey.

Experiment has continually driven this progress. Rutherford’s scattering experiment

revealed the nuclear structure of the atom [1], soon after came the discoveries of the neu-

tron [2], the positron [3], and later the neutrino [4] - an initially elusive particle introduced

to preserve conservation laws. By the mid-20th century, dozens of new particles were being

observed in cosmic-ray and accelerator experiments, forming a “zoo” of hadrons that de-

manded a unifying structure. Gell-Mann’s eight-fold way [5] and the quark model brought

order to this complexity through symmetry principles. Noether’s theorem [6], linking sym-

metries to conserved quantities, provided deep theoretical guidance, while group theory

became the mathematical backbone of modern particle physics.

These developments culminated in the electroweak theory of Glashow, Weinberg and

Salam [7, 8], unified by gauge symmetry and spontaneous symmetry breaking. The dis-



2

covery of the Higgs boson in 2012 [9, 10, 11] completed this framework and confirmed the

mechanism responsible for generating particle masses. Together, these achievements form

the Standard Model - a remarkably elegant and successful theory of fundamental particles

and interactions. It accurately describes a vast range of phenomena, from precision elec-

troweak measurements to the behavior of quarks and leptons at high energies. Despite its

success, the SM is incomplete.

One of the most compelling pieces of evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model

is dark matter, whose gravitational effects are well established but its particle nature

remains unknown. A promising possibility is that dark matter can be produced in high

energy particle collisions, where it would manifest as missing transverse momentum. In

this thesis, we search for dark matter produced in proton-proton collisions at the LHC at a

center of mass energy of 13 TeV in Run-2 data taking period of the CMS experiment. This

analysis looks for statistically significant deviations from the Standard Model predictions,

either enhancements in specific kinematic regions or excesses resembling a bump-hunt

signature.



3

Chapter 2

The Standard Model

The field of particle physics has been remarkably successful in advancing our understand-

ing of the fundamental laws governing the Universe. With the discovery of the Higgs

boson, the Standard Model of particle physics is a self-consistent experimentally validated

framework describing the known fundamental constituents of matter and their interac-

tions. It provides a coherent description of quarks, leptons, gauge bosons, and the Higgs

field, and it has withstood decades of increasingly precise experimental tests.

Despite its tremendous success, the Standard Model is widely recognized as an in-

complete theory. It does not incorporate gravity, nor does it account for the observed

dark matter and dark energy in the universe. These and other open questions provide

compelling reasons for physics beyond the Standard Model, motivating both theoretical

developments and a broad experimental program aimed at uncovering new particles and

interactions.

Before exploring these extensions and the broader search program for new physics, it is

useful to review the key features of the Standard Model, the elegant theory that currently

forms the foundation of particle physics.



4

2.1 Particles and Interactions

The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics is a quantum field theory that describes

the fundamental particles and three of the four known fundamental forces, excluding

gravity. It incorporates the principles of quantum mechanics and special relativity through

the language of relativistic quantum field theory, with its dynamics encoded in the SM

Lagrangian.

The SM includes the electromagnetic, weak, and strong nuclear interactions. These

forces arise from underlying gauge symmetries: a U(1)Y symmetry associated with hyper-

charge, an SU(2)L symmetry for the weak interaction, and an SU(3)C symmetry for Quan-

tum Chromodynamics (QCD), the theory of the strong force. The electromagnetic and

the weak force are unified under the electroweak theory, described by the SU(2)L×U(1)Y

gauge group. After electroweak symmetry breaking, this gauge structure gives rise to the

photon, W±, and Z bosons.

Within this framework, the fundamental particles are excitations of the underlying

quantum fields. They fall into two categories: fermions which are building blocks of

matter, and bosons which are the mediators of interactions. The fermions have spin
1

while gauge bosons have spin 1. The SM also contains a single fundamental scalar particle,

the Higgs boson with spin 0. The Higgs field is responsible for electroweak symmetry

breaking, which generates masses for the W and Z bosons through the Brout-Englert-

Higgs mechanism [12, 8, 13]. Fermions get their mass through the Yukawa coupling to the

Higgs field. The Higgs boson itself acquire mass from the self-interaction with the Higgs

field.

Each SM particle is characterized by a set of quantum numbers, including its invariant

mass, electric charge (in units of e), spin and additional internal charges such has color,

weak isospin, and hypercharge. Figure 2.1 illustrates the particle content of the SM,

arranged according to their quantum properties. The first three columns contain the

fermions organized into three generations, which share identical properties except their

masses. The fourth column contains the gauge or vector bosons: the photon γ, gluon g,



5

and the W and Z bosons that mediate the electromagnetic, strong and weak interactions,

respectively. Finally the fifth column shows the scalar Higgs boson.

2.1.1 The electroweak interaction

The weak nuclear interaction is responsible for processes such as nuclear beta decay and

flavor-changing transitions among quarks and leptons. It is mediated by three massive

gauge bosons - the charged W± and the neutral Z and is unique among the fundamental

interactions in several respects: it violates parity, it is the only interaction that changes

quark and lepton flavor, and its mediators are massive, giving it an extremely short range

compared to electromagnetism.

The weak interaction is described within the framework of an SU(2)L gauge symmetry,

where the subscript L denotes that the gauge bosons couple exclusively to left-handed

2.1.2 Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking and the Higgs mechanism

The electroweak theory described in the previous section presents an immediate tension.

The SU(2)L×U(1)Y gauge symmetry, as written, requires all gauge bosons to be massless,

just as gauge invariance forces the photon to be massless in QED. Yet the W± and Z

bosons are observed to be massive, with mW ≈ 80 GeV and mZ ≈ 91 GeV. A naive

resolution to add an explicit mass term m2WµW
µ to the Lagrangian explicitly breaks

gauge invariance and destroys the renormalization of the theory, leading to non-unitary

scattering amplitudes and mathematical inconsistencies at high energies. A more subtle

mechanism is therefore required, one that generates gauge boson masses without explicitly

breaking the underlying symmetry [15].



8

Historical path to the solution

The foundation was laid in 1954, when Yang and Mills formulated the first non-Abelian

gauge theory based on SU(2) [16]. Glashow subsequently extended this to an SU(2)L ×

U(1)Y gauge structure to describe the unified electroweak interaction [12], but the question

of how to give the W and Z bosons mass while preserving gauge invariance remained

unresolved.

A key insight came from condensed matter physics. In 1950, Ginzburg and Landau

proposed a macroscopic description of superconductivity in terms of spontaneous breaking

of the electromagnetic gauge symmetry. A microscopic understanding followed in 1957

with the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory [17, 18], which described the formation

of Cooper pairs. Anderson noted in 1963 that in a superconductor, electromagnetic waves

below a certain plasma frequency behave as if the photon acquires a mass, and suggested

that an analogous mechanism could operate in a relativistic gauge theory to give mass to

gauge bosons without violating gauge invariance [19].

Building on this insight, Brout and Englert [20], and independently Higgs [13, 21,

22], demonstrated how spontaneous symmetry breaking of a relativistic scalar field could

generate masses for gauge bosons in a fully consistent manner. This mechanism, now

known as the Brout-Englert-Higgs (BEH) mechanism, is the cornerstone of the electroweak

theory. The renormalisability of the resulting theory was rigorously established in 1971 by

’t Hooft and Veltman [23], elevating the electroweak model of Glashow [12], Weinberg [8],

and Salam [7, 24, 25] to a complete and well-defined quantum field theory. The subsequent

experimental confirmation of the W and Z bosons at CERN in 1983 provided decisive

validation of this framework.

Spontaneous symmetry breaking

The Lagrangian LHiggs is fully invariant under SU(2)L × U(1)Y gauge transformations.

However, the ground state of the theory must select a specific point from the degenerate

circle of minima, and this selection breaks the symmetry. This is the essence of spontaneous

symmetry breaking. It is a property of the vacuum state, not of the Lagrangian itself. The

theory retains its gauge invariance at the level of the action; it is the ground state that is

not symmetric.

Yukawa interaction

The gauge boson masses generated by the BEH mechanism arise from the covariant kinetic

term of the scalar doublet, as shown in the previous section. However, explicit fermion

mass terms of the form mψ̄LψR are forbidden in the SM, since ψL and ψR transform

differently under SU(2)L and such a term would break gauge invariance. Instead, fermion

2.1.4 The Higgs boson

The discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC in 2012, independently announced by the

ATLAS and CMS collaborations [9, 10, 11], marked the completion of the SM particle

content and a landmark achievement in experimental particle physics. With a measured

mass of mH ≈ 125 GeV, the Higgs boson is the only fundamental scalar particle observed

in nature, and its properties provide a unique window into the mechanism of electroweak

symmetry breaking.

As established in the previous section, the Higgs boson couples to all massive SM

particles with a strength proportional to their mass: to gauge bosons as m2
V /ν and to

fermions as mf/ν. This mass-proportional coupling structure determines both the pro-

constitutes the primary set of experimental predictions tested.

At hadron colliders such as the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, the Higgs boson can

be produced through several mechanisms. The dominant production mode is gluon-gluon

fusion (ggF), mediated by a top-quark loop. Other significant channels include vector

boson fusion (VBF), associated production with a vector boson (VH), and associated

production with a top-quark pair (tt̄H). The corresponding Feynman diagrams are shown

in Figure 2.3 (top). Each production mechanism probes different aspects of the Higgs

interactions and allows complementary tests of the SM.

The Higgs boson decays into various final states, with its branching ratios determined

2.2 Limitations of the Standard Model

The Standard Model, despite its remarkable predictive power and experimental success,

is widely understood to be an incomplete description of nature. Several well-established

observational facts and theoretical considerations cannot be accommodated within its cur-

rent framework, providing compelling motivation for physics beyond the Standard Model.

One of the most significant motivations is discussed here.

Dark Matter and Dark Energy

Astrophysical and cosmological observations provide overwhelming evidence for the exis-

tence of a non-luminous, non-baryonic form of matter “dark matter” that interacts gravi-

tationally. Evidence comes from multiple independent observations, one of which indicate

that dark matter constitutes approximately 27% of the total energy density of the Uni-

verse. The SM offers no viable dark matter candidate — none of its particles has the right

combination of stability, mass, and interaction strength to account for the observed relic

density. Equally puzzling is the observed accelerated expansion of the Universe, attributed

to a form of energy “dark energy” that permeates space uniformly and acts as a repul-

sive contribution to gravity. Dark energy is estimated to constitute approximately 68%

of the total energy density of the Universe, with ordinary baryonic matter accounting for

only about 5%. The SM provides no explanation for dark energy, and its origin remains

one of the deepest unsolved problems in fundamental physics. Together, dark matter and



18

dark energy account for approximately 95% of the total energy content of the Universe,

underscoring the severe limitations of the SM as a complete description of nature.

The SM describes three of the four known fundamental forces — the electromagnetic,

weak, and strong interactions — within a unified quantum field theoretical framework.

Gravity, however, is not incorporated. General relativity provides an extraordinarily suc-

cessful classical description of gravitation, but all attempts to quantize it in the same

manner as the other interactions encounter fundamental difficulties. The resulting the-

ory is non-renormalisable, producing ultraviolet divergences at energies approaching the

Planck scale.

The hierarchy between the electroweak scale and the Planck scale is itself a theoretical

puzzle, known as the hierarchy problem: quantum corrections to the Higgs boson mass

are quadratically sensitive to any new physics scale up to the Planck mass, requiring an

extraordinary degree of fine-tuning to keep mH ≈ 125 GeV.

Taken together, these limitations paint a consistent picture: the SM is a highly suc-

cessful effective theory valid up to currently accessible energy scales, but it is not a com-

plete description of nature. The existence of dark matter is among the most direct and

well-evidenced of these shortcomings, and it forms the central motivation for the analysis

presented in this thesis.



19

Chapter 3

Beyond the Standard Model

Despite the tremendous success of the SM at predicting and explaining the elementary

particles and their interactions, it does not incorporate all the observed phenomena in the

universe. For instance, the problem of dark matter is not described within the SM as none

of the particles have the right properties that could make up the DM [29].

3.1 Observational evidence for dark matter

There has been compelling evidence through various observations that hint the presence

of dark matter. The composition of the universe is a central question of astrophysics and

cosmology. A large and diverse set of observations suggest the existence of a significant

amount of non-luminous matter. The nature and origin of this matter are some of the

most exciting questions in fundamental physics [30].

Light neutrinos are relativistic and can not account for DM. If the DM particles

were produced in the early universe, these particles have to be ‘cold’, which means non-

relativistic at the time of galaxy formation. However, neutrinos set the stage for the

hypothetical particles known as WIMPs - weakly interacting massive particles [31].

These observations led to the construction of Cosmological Standard Model, called

the “Lambda CDM” model [32], which assumes a cold dark matter with a cosmological

constant (Λ).



20

3.1.1 Galaxy rotation curve

The first modern indication of unseen mass in the universe came from the pioneering work

of Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s [33]. He applied the Virial theorem and used the dispersion

velocity of galaxies in the Coma cluster to estimate their mass from gravitational poten-

tial. He also estimated the mass of the visible galaxies from luminosity measurements, and

compared the two masses. He found a stark discrepancy: the visible mass from luminosity

measurements was too little to account for the observed velocities. To resolve this incon-

sistency, he proposed the existence of non-luminous or “dark” matter that would provide

the additional gravitational pull required to speed up the orbits.

Further compelling evidence emerged in the 1970s from the study of galaxy rotation

curves. In optical observations, Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured the rotation speeds of

stars in spiral galaxies and found that they remained unexpectedly high at large radii [34].

Around the same time, radio telescopes were used to map the 21 cm line of interstellar

atomic hydrogen in Andromeda galaxy, which extended the curve to larger radial distances,

much beyond the optical measurements. The velocity curve did not decline as expected

from Keplerian orbits, but was observed to be flat, suggesting very large values of mass-

to-luminosity ratio in the outer parts of the extended disks. Figure 3.1 shows the galactic

rotation curve for NGC 6503, with contributions from the visible stars in the galactic disk

and gas are shown, along with the DM halo contribution which is needed to match the

observed data. The rotation curve observation is limited to distances of few tens of kpc

as one needs light or interstellar hydrogen 21 cm line.

3.1.2 Gravitational lensing

Einstein’s general theory of relativity predicts that massive objects curve the spacetime,

and light follows these curved paths. As a result, when light from a distant source passes

near a massive object such as another galaxy or cluster, its path is bent and to an observer

on Earth, the background source may appear distorted, magnified, or even split into several

images. This effect is known as gravitational lensing. This effect can be used to detect



21

gas as a function of their radial distance from the galaxy center. The DM halo contribution
needed to match the data is also shown. Figure taken from [35].

mass even when it does not emit any light, as lensing depends only on gravity, not on the

luminosity of the intervening matter.

Strong gravitational lensing occurs when the distorted background galaxies appear

as multiple distinct images, arcs, or even complete Einstein rings. By measuring the

geometry of such distortions, one can estimate the mass of the intervening massive object.

Observations of galaxy clusters often show that the total mass required to produce such

strong lensing features is several times larger than what can be accounted for by luminous

matter alone, suggesting presence of a massive dark matter halo.

When the alignment between the observer, lens, and background source is less perfect,

the deflection angles are small, and individual distortions may be too subtle to detect in a

single galaxy image. With a large statistical sample of millions of background galaxies, one

can measure a coherent pattern. Large surveys such as the Dark Energy Survey (DES)



22

have used this technique to construct detailed “mass maps” of the sky, which reveal a

cosmic web structure. The matter, dominated by dark matter forms clusters, filaments

and voids, that closely match the predictions from ΛCDM cosmology model.

A striking and widely cited example is the bullet cluster (1E 0657-56) [36], a system

formed by the collision of two galaxy clusters, shown in Figure 3.2.

During this collision event, the inter-cluster gaseous medium (shown in pink), which

is mostly baryonic matter, interacts electromagnetically emitting X-rays. This region

is where the center of mass lies based on X-ray observations, and lags behind the sub-

gravitationally slowed by the collision and not significantly affected.

Based on gravitational lensing effects, the center of mass lies in the blue colored region

which bypassed the gaseous region during the collision. This suggests that most of the

mass is in fact collisionless dark matter and does not interact electromagnetically.



23

Gravitational lensing provides a direct and model-independent way to probe dark

matter. It does not rely on assumptions about equilibrium or cosmic evolution. It simply

measures the gravitational effects of matter, and these observations have so far implied

that dark matter is the dominant form of matter in the universe.

3.1.3 Cosmic Microwave Background

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) [38] is one of the most powerful piece of evi-

dence for the existence of dark matter. It also provides an estimate of the content of DM

in the universe. In the big bang cosmological model, the early universe was filled with

opaque, dense, hot plasma of sub-atomic particles. Approximately 380,000 years after

the big bang, as the universe expanded and cooled, the protons and electrons combined

to form neutral atoms, mostly hydrogen. This event made the universe transparent to

radiation as the photons were no longer scattered off of free electrons, and could travel

freely through space. Those photons are what we now observe as the CMB in the mi-

crowave region, which can still be detected today as a faint signal in the universe with a

temperature of around 2.72 Kelvin. As the universe expands, the CMB photons are red-

shifted and decrease in energy. The CMB is very smooth and uniform but contains very

small temperature fluctuations, at the level of one part in 105. These anisotropies carry

detailed information about the composition and geometry of the early universe, reflecting

the interplay between gravitational collapse and radiation pressure in the plasma, setting

up acoustic oscillations [39], [40]. Experiments such as WMAP and Planck have taken

high-precision measurements with a sky map. This can be decomposed into an angular

power spectrum. The positions and relative heights of the acoustic peaks in the power

spectrum can be analyzed to determine the matter content of the universe.

In this model, the dark matter does not directly interact with radiation, but affects

the CMB by its gravitational pull and by its effects on the density and velocity of ordinary

matter. As a result, the first (and other odd-numbered) acoustic peaks in the CMB power

spectrum are enhanced relative to the even-numbered ones — a clear signature that a non-

The precise measurements of the CMB anisotropies constrain the total matter density and

3.2 Implications for dark matter models

The various astrophysical and cosmological observations that imply the existence of dark

matter also constrain its physical properties [43, 44]. Although we do not yet know what

dark matter is made of, we have learned a lot about what it cannot be.

First, DM does not have electromagnetic charge since it does not emit, absorb, or

reflect light to any detectable degree, otherwise it would have been observed in optical,

radio, or X-ray surveys. Moreover, DM must be non-baryonic. The baryon density inferred

from the CMB is much smaller than the total matter density required to explain cosmic

structure formation, implying that the bulk matter is not made of protons or neutrons.



25

Second, the bullet cluster observation emphasizes that DM does not hold a color charge

since that would lead to strong interactions between the DM and baryonic matter, which

would cause DM to clump more tightly than what was observed. If DM could interact

via the strong force, the structure of galaxies and galaxy clusters would have been differ-

ent [45]. DM must be massive and gravitationally interacting. Its presence is detected

only through its gravitational effects. To provide the gravitational potential well that

seeded the formation of galaxies and clusters, DM must dominate the matter budget of

the universe.

Third, DM must be non-relativistic (“cold” DM) during the cosmic structure forma-

tion. If DM particles were very-light, or relativistic (“hot” DM), small scale structures

would have been washed out, contradicting the observed abundance of galaxies and clus-

ters. Measurements of the CMB anisotropies also suggest that DM must be cold during

the early universe.

Fourth, DM must be long-lived and stable on the cosmological timescales. Since its

gravitational effects are observed from the CMB to present day, DM particles can not

decay into standard particles. Indirect detection experiments that search for decay of DM

have placed a constraint on the lifetime of DM.

Any successful dark matter model will have to satisfy all of these observations and

constraints. Over the past few decades, many theoretical frameworks have been proposed

to explain the nature of DM. Several well-motivated classes of candidates emerge natu-

rally from extensions of the SM. Figure 3.4 shows the DM candidates, from particles to

primordial black holes, and their allowed mass range.

3.2.1 Weakly Interacting Massive Particles

This is the most widely studied candidate model, which predicts particles with masses

in the range of 10 GeV to several TeV that interact through the weak nuclear force or

some version of it [47, 48]. The WIMPs [31, 49] are massive, stable, electrically neutral

particles that interact via the weak force with the SM. One of the most appealing aspects

freeze-out. In the hot, dense conditions of the early universe, WIMPs would have been in

thermal equilibrium with SM particles, constantly being created and annihilated in pair

χ+ χ̄←→ f + f̄ (3.1)

where χ denotes the WIMP and f the SM particle. As the universe expanded and

cooled to temperatures below the WIMP mass, the average energy of the SM particles

WIMP particles would have continued, and the density would begin to decrease expo-

predicted relic abundance coincides strikingly well with the dark matter density measured

by the Planck satellite. This remarkable coincidence is called the WIMP miracle [43],

which suggests that the DM problem might be connected to physics at the electroweak

This has motivated a wide range of theoretical models in which WIMPs appear nat-

duces a symmetry between fermions and bosons. In SUSY models that conserve R-parity,

the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) is stable and can serve as a WIMP candi-

date [47]. In many scenarios, this is the neutralino, a combination of the SUSY partners

of the photon, Z boson and neutral Higgs boson.

3.3 Experimental searches for dark matter

WIMPs have testable consequences that make them particularly attractive. Under the

assumption of weak interactions between WIMPs and SM particles, they can potentially

be detected in three complementary methods, as illustrated in Figure 3.5.

1. Direct detection, by observing nuclear recoils from WIMP scattering in underground

detectors such as XENONnT [51], LZ [52], or PandaX [53].

2. Indirect detection, by searching for the products of WIMP annihilation or decay,

such as gamma rays, positrons, or neutrinos, from regions of high DM density with

experiments such as Fermi-LAT [54], and IceCube [55].

3. Collider production, by creating WIMPs in high-energy collisions, such as those

at the LHC, where they would escape detection and be inferred by presence of

missing transverse momentum. Such searches look for WIMPs produced alongside

SM particles like jet, photon, or Higgs boson.

These methods have different advantages and limitations but are complementary ap-

proaches and together provide a more complete picture of DM constraints [56]. The direct

and indirect detection experiments can probe relic particle DM that can provide insights

into the nature of DM halos, while the collider experiments can study DM production and

offer insights into DM interactions in early universe.



28

3.3.1 Direct detection

The idea is to detect the DM particles (e.g WIMPs) passing through the Earth that may

occasionally scatter off nuclei in a sensitive detector. These look for low energy (typically

few keV) recoils of nuclei which emit energy in the form of scintillation light. The expected

interaction rates are extremely small and the energy deposits are very low, because of which

these experiments are carefully designed to maximize the signal while minimizing the

background. These experiments typically operate deep underground, where interference

from cosmic background is minimal.

If a DM particle, eg. WIMP were to scatter off a nucleus in a sensitive detector, it

would impart a small amount of energy to the nucleus, producing a measurable recoil.

Detecting these rare nuclear recoils requires instruments that are capable of observing

energy deposits of few to 100 keV. The expected event rate is extremely small, often less

than one interaction per tonne of detector material per year. Therefore, these experiments

rely on massive detectors, extremely low background contamination and careful shielding

to suppress all known forms of noise.

The choice of target material is crucial, these experiments use highly pure noble liquids

such as xenon or argon since they provide large, homogeneous detector volume and allow

simultaneous measurement of scintillation light and ionization signals. This dual-channel



29

readout enables experiments to distinguish nuclear recoils from the far more common

electronic recoils caused by background radiation. Other experimental approaches use

cryogenic germanium or silicon crystals, which can measure phonon (heat) and ionization

signals with exquisite precision, or NaI(Tl) crystals designed to look for annual modulation

effects in the dark matter flux.

Since the expected signal is very rare, the ultimate goal is to increase the total exposure,

defined as the product of detector mass and live-time, while maintaining ultra-low back-

grounds and low energy thresholds. The frontier of the field has been steadily advancing,

with each generation of experiments improving both sensitivity and target mass. The cur-

rent leaders, such as LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) in the Sanford Underground Research Facility and

XENONnT at Gran Sasso, use multi-tonne liquid-xenon time projection chambers (TPCs)

that can reconstruct event positions in three dimensions and discriminate background in-

teractions with high efficiency. These detectors are sensitive to WIMP masses from a

few GeV up to several TeV. Figure 3.6 shows the upper limits on the spin-independent

WIMP-nucleon cross section set by various experiments as a function of the WIMP DM

mass. Direct detection experiments are usually limited by the uncertainty in the scatter-

ing of the nucleus with neutrinos coming from solar and atmospheric sources. This is an

irreducible background because the nuclear recoil energy spectra of these events closely

resembles the DM signature.

3.3.2 Indirect detection

While direct detection experiments aim to observe dark matter scattering locally, indirect

detection seeks evidence of dark matter interactions on cosmic scales — through the sec-

ondary particles produced when dark matter annihilates or decays [59, 60]. If dark matter

particles annihilate or decay into Standard Model particles (or produce them in cascade),

one may detect photons (especially gamma-rays), cosmic-ray antiparticles (positrons, an-

tiprotons), or neutrinos from regions of high DM density.

For a stable DM candidate that self-annihilates, the annihilation rate scales roughly

Gamma-rays are a particularly clean channel because they travel in straight lines (ig-

neutrinos can escape dense environments. Charged cosmic rays, like positrons and antipro-

tons, can carry signature features but are affected by propagation and solar modulation,

and can complicate the interpretation. Some of the most common astrophysical targets

for indirect detection include Dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) of the Milky Way, the

galactic center, and galaxy clusters.

Neutrinos offer a complementary and unique window because they can escape dense

environments unattenuated. WIMPs could accumulate and annihilate inside massive celes-

tial bodies such as the Sun or Earth, producing neutrinos that could be detected by large-

scale neutrino telescopes. Experiments like IceCube at the South Pole and ANTARES in

the Mediterranean have searched for excesses of neutrinos coming from the direction of



31

the Sun, but so far none have been observed. These null results translate into limits on

the WIMP–nucleon scattering cross section that are complementary to those from direct

detection, especially for spin-dependent interactions.

To date, no unambiguous signal of DM annihilation or decay has been established via

indirect detection. Instead, many experiments have set upper limits on annihilation cross

example, the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT) has performed combined analyses

of multiple Milky Way dwarf satellite galaxies (for instance, 25 dwarfs in one study)

and found no significant gamma-ray excess consistent with common WIMP annihilation
